The spirit of gift-giving is not a static, frozen one. No, it’s one filled with dynamism, energy, verve, and excitement—much like the holiday season itself. It’s bristling with unbridled feelings of joy and goodwill, almost jittery with anticipation. It’s practically bouncing off the walls like, well, a child on Christmas morning creeping down the stairs to gaze lovingly at the rich landscape of gifts spilling forth from the glittering tree.

And so this year we sought out gifts that matched the moment. Gifts that would swing, dangle, bounce, roll, rock, and more. To capture them in still lives was not to honor their form. And so, we decided to make not a gift guide, but a .gif guide, to imbue these wonderful baubles and delights with the vivacious momentum they so deserve. So take a gander at our favorite gifts of the season, now vibrating and twitching with life.

And with that, we present you with the Vogue 2026 .Gif Guide.

With its hinged cover, this compact swings open to reveal its hydrating and shimmering lip gloss. The perfect little reveal when you and your lips are feeling a bit dull.

Thanks to its structured top, metallic-frame closure, dainty handle, and soft lambskin body, this darling handbag is demure and alluring, but its squishy body gives it an unexpected dimension worthy of a hug.

Chanel’s fabulous shoes have become an instant best-seller, thanks to their fresh prints and whimsical use of color. Just imagine traipsing around town in these animal-print heels with their pop-of-red toes. You’ll get double takes for all the right reasons.

#6763. The 15 Best Chelsea Boots for Men in 2026: Never Go Out of Style

The best Chelsea boots for men are trend-proof in a way that'll make you breathe a sigh of relief. Especially right now, when menswear feels like a WWE Royal Rumble, where anything goes and trends pile up like bodies in and out of the ring. But there, floating confidently above everything, is the trustworthy Chelsea boot.

If we had to make an educated guess as to why the Chelsea boot has stuck around for so long? Good design is good design. The slip-on simplicity, the sharp silhouette, the unadorned, uncomplicated details—the pared-back design makes it highly adaptable to any wardrobe and occasion, trends be damned. So don't be ashamed to cash in on a fleeting fad, but when it comes time for you to do some spring cleaning, we'd advise against letting go of a pair of Chelseas.

We've rounded up 15 of the best Chelsea boots out there, from hardwearing stompers to exquisite stunners, $200 steals to $1,500 beauties. Finding the perfect pair can be hard—but pulling them on? Easy.

Ask us what Chelsea boot you should get, regardless of price, and we'll point to the R.M. Williams Turnout boot, because it does so many things right that the competition can't. Off the bat, it’s a real stunner. The silhouette is sleek and chiseled, timeless and fashion forward. The leather is perfectly suited for a shine and polish to attend any black tie event, but takes on a handsome patina when worn hard. Plus, the quality is fantastic. The wholecut leather uppers are shaped as a single piece of cowhide rather than several panels stitched together, resulting in a shoe that’s as pretty as it is durable. With Goodyear-welted construction for easy peasy resoling, you’ll have these Aussie-born boots for well over a decade.

How does a boot originally built for Down Under cowboys manage to be the best-looking dress boot and hardest-wearing boot at the same time? Hard to say. The only drawback of the R.M. Williams Heritage Craftsman Chelsea is the price. But considering everything it can do—and how long it'll last—the math makes sense.

For the budget conscious/the dude looking for his first pair of “nice” Chelsea boots, my answer is easy: Beckett Simonon. Menswear bros might scoff at a web-only DTC clothing brand, but unlike the other brands with infinite marketing budgets looking to “disrupt the entire industry”, Beckett Simonon seems content with making great shoes at a great price, without all the soulless millennial pandering. The Bolton, a slick sleek, true-to-form  Chelsea boot, is just the poster child for the brand’s modus operandi. It uses full-grain Italian calfskin, which is lined with Vachetta leather, stitched by master shoemakers in Columbia using a Blake stitch construction.

In other words, it’s a Chelsea boot with A-list looks, Northamptonshire-style pedigree, and a price that’s at least half of the competition. But if there’s one thing that will stop most people from buying a pair immediately is, well, you can’t get them immediately. Each pair is made to order, which means you’ll have to wait a month or two to get yours. But you know what they say: patience is a virtue.

Some Chelsea boots lean heavily into their rockstar appeal, while others skew utilitarian, expressly designed to protect you from the elements. Then there, however, are the rare pairs that gracefully straddle the line between. Enter the other Australian boot: Blundstone. Those tough leather uppers might not be monsoon-ready, but on days when you just need to jump a few puddles en route to work, the whole package is the slickest way to ensure your socks stay dry without compromising your fit.

Tired Bushwick memes aside, Blunnies are truly good looking boots built like a tank. They can take a real whooping and still show up for their 5 a.m. shift behind the espresso machine, ready for more. They’re a boot you don’t have to feel precious about, and the de facto kicks to wear when the weather forecast just says “shitty.” They look great with vintage jeans, a pair of Dickies, cargo pants, and chinos—though, in our humble opinion, they don't belong anywhere with a dress code (explicit or implied).

Hedi Slimane’s legacy at Saint Laurent was all skinny jeans, razor-sharp suits, and rockstar Chelsea boots. The look he cooked up over a decade ago has come back again, with guys dubbing themselves Hedi Boys looking to recreate the magic. One glance at boots like these, and you understand why. A leading man gleam and a stacked Cuban heel mean these boots by themselves could headline Coachella. The only update: a very right-now edginess (literally) at the toe. Whether or not the rumored skinny jeans comeback arrives, these are the boots to wear when you want all eyes on you.

Astorflex has long been one of the best value propositions in the shoe space. The Tuscan vegetable-tanned leather and multigenerational craftsmanship alone should be worth more than what you'll actually pay. But value doesn't equate to style. Thankfully, the Bitflex has that in spades. Not too pointy and not totally bulbous, the shape splits the difference masterfully and looks great paired with any kind of pants. Plus, the cushioned crepe sole plays down the dressy factor while adding a ton of comfort straight out of the box.

Unlike other crepe-soled boots more famous than these—ahem—these don’t feel suspiciously soft, despite their extremely comfortable feel. In my experience, Astorflex boots maintain great arch support and mold to your feet, but also are built up enough to provide some noticeable ankle support. This is certainly the most casual Chelsea boot here, so don’t even think of trying to wear these to your friend’s wedding. You’re not “doing something”, you’re being disrespectful.

If you think of Red Wing, it's the brand’s iconic 6-inch moc toe boots you’re probably imagining. But the Minnesotan boot makers can do more than turn out jobsite-endorsed footwear. Introduced in the 1990s, Red Wing’s Chelseas were made for ranchers who wanted something durable enough for the farm, but easy enough to nap in. They’re a happy middle ground between a high-shine European Chelsea like the R.M. Williams and the woodsy Blundstones.

That means you get Goodyear-welted construction and built-to-stroll rubber outsoles topped by Hawthorne Muleskinner roughout suede. The texture is “rugged handyman,” but the dusty tan and dark brown color can hold down a coffee date-worthy fit. White tees and white jeans? Sure. Nice pants and a knit sweater or polo? Absolutely. Wranglers and a Stetson. Of course.

Morjas is best known for loafers worn by everyone from Wall Street bros to Greenpoint baristas. Now the Swedish shoemakers are coming for your ankles with a Chelsea boot. If you’ve already graduated from Chelsea Boots 101 by having a classic black or brown calf-leather pair in your closet, consider these brown suede beauties for next semester.

They're fully leather-lined but require absolutely zero break-in time, thanks to a studded rubber sole that feels like walking on a cloud... if clouds had traction. Style-wise, they walk the line (pun intended) between office-ready and weekend cool—equally dialed in when paired with a crisp white dress shirt beneath unforgiving Monday-morning fluorescents or some linen pants while you sip a doppia espresso in Florence.

You already know what that yellow stitching means. Dr. Martens’ chunky, iconic boots bring an EVA insole and the brand's patented oil- and slip-resistant AirWair sole to the water-resistant oiled leather. Add a pull tab for easy entry, and the only thing easier than slipping them on is adding them to cart when you realize they’re on sale.

By cutting out the middleman and selling direct-to-consumer, Meermin offers handsome, Goodyear-welted dress shoes—all made from leather with absurdly tony provenances—for well below what the other guys charge. You can’t go wrong with any of the brand’s boots, but a mocha-hued suede Chelsea looks especially killer in the fall.

Blundstones again, you say? Well, yes. But this pair has a leather lining and plusher sole, which make them both more comfortable and longer lasting, if for a slightly higher price.

From the rugged to the refined. Chelsea boots are named after London's affluent Chelsea neighbourhood, and this model from British quality shoemakers Crockett & Jones' lives up to that name perhaps more than any on this list.

The Spanish shoe-whisperers at Camper fly a little under the radar compared to their British counterparts, but their Chelsea boots offer just as much swaggering rock-god energy as any other pair on this list. Thanks to a cushy OrthoLite footbed, though, you can wear ‘em long after Mick Jagger takes his final bow.

The chatter about Our Legacy's Camion boots never seems to end. That handsome silhouette, the '90s-esque square toe, and the slick side zip make these a modern-day classic.

Viberg makes boots on steroids in its family-owned Canadian factory, turning out museum-worthy footwear designed to stomp through the worst the world—or the ground, at least—has to offer. These Chelseas are cut from a single piece of waxed leather, like a Barbour jacket for your feet.

NYC-based 3sixteen has been on an absolute footwear tear lately—first with its slick Saucony collab, and now with a lug-soled Chelsea boot that stands on business. The whole shoe smashes together slightly disparate details—an elegant tobacco-colored suede, a workmanlike wedge lugged sole, an skyscraper-height ankle—that add up to something fresh in the normally staid world of Chelsea boots. And if you’ve ever broken in a pair of 3sixteen’s top-tier jeans, you already know: things only get better as you put in the steps.

Chelsea boots have always looked cool—anywhere, on anyone, at any time. They were invented in the 1800s, but won their cultural cred later: the Beatles gave them a massive co-sign in the ’60s, then Hedi Slimane anchored his Saint Laurent rocker suits with them while rappers stacked their denim on top of Chelsea boots during the 2010s.

Which goes to show that Chelsea boots work with damn near anything in your closet, from your favorite Levi’s to baggy chinos to louche suits—even crew socks and shorts, depending on the boots and your taste for channeling some Pacific Northwest crunchiness. For more, check out our guide on how to wear Chelsea boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6762. All the Ways Princess Kate Paid Tribute to Queen Elizabeth II and Princess Diana on Remembrance Day

As the future queen of England, Princess Catherine will always bring a little piece of history with her.

Over the weekend, the British royal family celebrated Remembrance Day—a national day of memorial to honor service members and civilians who died in World War I, World War II, and subsequent military conflicts. For the two-day occasion, Kate dressed in elegant black looks, which she accessorized with layers of meaningful pieces.

On Saturday, to attend the Royal British Legion Festival of Remembrance event at London’s Royal Albert Hall, Kate slipped on a black-and-white polka-dot dress by Alessandra Rich, and added some sparkle with Queen Elizabeth II’s Orbital pendant earrings. The late monarch first publicly wore the two-tier diamond earrings to the state opening of parliament in May 2012, and later loaned them to Kate in 2016. The princess inherited the jewelry after the queen’s passing in 2022.

Top top off her dotted look, Kate pinned on a red poppy brooch from Izzy Ager of Lock & Co. (The poppy is a symbol of Remembrance Day.), and her Irish Guards Regimental Brooch.

On Sunday, the Princess of Wales stepped out in a sophisticated black Catherine Walker coat (one of her favorites), that she adorned with her HMS Glasgow brooch and three red poppies. She also brought a little of the late Princess Diana with her for the special day by accessorizing with Lady Di’s famous Collingwood pearl drop earrings. Each earring features a diamond stud and a diamond bell cap atop a shiny white pearl. The pieces were gifted to Diana in 1981, for her wedding to then-Prince Charles, by London jeweler Collingwood (a favorite of the Spencer family).

#6760. ‘Love Is Blind’ Star Rob Feeley Releases Lengthy Statement, Claims Fans Saw “a Small Part of a Much Bigger Experience”

Love Is Blind Season 11 star Rob Feeley is breaking his silence after a truly messy season. Quick recap: Rob got engaged to Michaella Giorgio in the Pods, but things went south during a cast-wide bar hang, where Rob told everyone he didn’t care about their relationship. Obviously, Michaella ended things, and Rob has some things to say now that he’s watched the season.

“Now that the reunion has aired and this chapter comes to a close, I’ve been reflecting on everything this experience has taught me,” Rob wrote on Instagram. “I’m truly grateful for the people I’ve met, the memories made, and the personal growth that came with both the incredible moments and the challenges. Looking back, there are moments I wish I had handled differently. There were times when I felt overwhelmed and let my emotions get the best of me. While those moments don’t reflect the person I strive to be, I recognize that they happened, and I take responsibility for how I reacted and where I could have communicated better.”

Rob went on to “acknowledge the hurt I caused Michaella,” saying “she deserved to feel heard, respected, and understood. I’m genuinely sorry for the times I fell short and for how I reacted in certain situations. My intentions don’t change the fact that my actions affected her, and I take responsibility for that.”

Rob also confirmed that he and Michaella have been in touch since the show filmed two (two!) years ago, and that they have moved on with “mutual respect.” He then reminded fans that they only saw “a small part of a much bigger experience, and not every conversation or situation can be fully understood from what makes it onto the screen.”

The burgeoning reality star ended his musings by teasing some “projects and opportunities” he’s been working on, and noted that “There’s a lot to look forward to in the coming weeks, and I’m excited to share what’s next.”

So...guess we’ll see what happens (next season of Perfect Match, perhaps?).

#6759. For More Volume and Less Oil, Start With These Dry Shampoos

I have fine hair and an oily scalp, which means a fresh wash looks great for about a day before my roots start to fall flat and my bangs give up on me. For years, I’d wash my hair every morning, until I realized all that shampooing and blow-drying could be swapped for something much easier—dry shampoo. A little at the roots on day two buys me another day or two between washes, and it’s saved more than one blowout I wasn’t ready to let go of. These days, a can lives on my vanity, another in my bag, and one permanently in my suitcase.

The reason it works so well comes down to what’s inside. Most formulas rely on ingredients like rice starch to soak up the oil sitting at your roots, which is what makes hair look fresh again, but getting rid of that oil also takes away the weight that makes roots fall flat in the first place. That’s why a good dry shampoo gives you a little lift almost instantly, and the powder leaves behind just enough texture to help a style hold without feeling stiff. If you’ve ever noticed that second-day hair is easier to style than freshly washed hair, that’s a big part of the reason.

Below, the best dry shampoos to use this season and beyond—according to the pros and Vogue editors.

Picking the perfect formula for your hair type makes all the difference. “All textures can use dry shampoo, but it may not be necessary or as beneficial for someone with coily hair,” says celebrity hairstylist Erinn Courtney. “Straight, wavy, or loosely curled hair benefits from dry shampoo most. Some dry shampoos are made for more oily hair, so they should be picked according to what kind of help your hair needs to feel fresh again.” Brooklyn-based hairstylist Mickiela Smith—also a trichologist and founder of hair-care platform—adds that for those with allergies or sensitive skin, it may be worth having a conversation with your doctor as they can provide a medicated, waterless shampoo to ease scalp woes.

Trichologist and colorist Bridgette Hill says that depending on hair type and texture, a dry shampoo can be used up to twice a day. “The important factor is ensuring there is a healthy hair care routine that balances the use of dry shampoo,” she notes. “If someone is using a dry shampoo daily, a proper shampoo with water should be performed at least every two to three days.” Board-certified dermatology nurse practitioner Catie Boucher reminds us that if we’re using dry shampoos regularly, it’s also essential to ensure we’re properly removing product buildup from our scalps during hair wash regimens. “I’ll be honest, I only wash my hair 1-2 times a week. I used to wash my hair daily, and not only did it not help with oiliness, it was a lot of work with long hair,” Boucher tells Vogue. “If you’re a dry shampoo loyalist like myself, or you use a lot of styling products, addressing product build-up with a scalp detox is never a bad idea.”

Dry shampoo can absolutely be part of a healthy haircare routine, as long as it’s used correctly and in moderation. “I see it as a styling and refreshing product rather than a replacement for washing your hair,” says Macias. “One of its biggest advantages is that it allows you to extend the life of a blowout or hairstyle, which can sometimes mean less frequent heat styling. From my professional perspective, that’s particularly useful when working with colored, fragile or heavily styled hair.” In any circumstance, the scalp always needs proper cleansing. “Using too much product or layering it repeatedly without washing can leave the scalp feeling uncomfortable and the hair looking dull,” warns Macias, who advises to only use dry shampoo where it’s needed, avoid overapplying and maintain a regular cleansing routine that suits your hair and scalp.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue's vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry's standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to dry shampoos, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, ease of application, spray vs non-aerosol, packaging, finish (ie: whether it leaves a white cast), and the hair-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6758. Amanda Seyfried Is So Sweet in a Shushu/Tong Babydoll Dress at the World Premiere of Steps

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

The babydoll dress has been making quite a comeback this year, thanks in large part to pop singer Olivia Rodrigo. Frequently inspired by the punk female rockers of the ’90s, Rodrigo sparked discourse and outrage this past spring while promoting her newest album in Peter Pan collar dresses and floral, pale-pink minis, which winked to forebears like Courtney Love and Kat Bjelland. Now, it seems she’s starting a revolution.

At the world premiere of her Netflix animated musical film, Steps, on Sunday evening, star Amanda Seyfried pulled out her own babydoll moment courtesy of Shanghai-based fashion label Shushu/Tong. The brand is known for its hyper-feminine styles inspired by retro aesthetics and art forms like anime, and those design hallmarks were on full display here.

Seyfried’s cropped, cream-colored dress featured a scoop neckline and spaghetti shoulder straps, with an empire waist and a ballooning skirt that added subtle volume, despite the little shape.

The material was made of a crinkly taffeta, and a pointy bow was attached right in the middle, under the bust, for a dainty finishing touch.

To match the dress, Seyfried wore a pair of satin pumps in a complementing eggshell, and she accessorized the look with jewelry from Tiffany & Co., including the Triple Drop link earrings, a Schlumberger ring, and a T1 ring in gold.

In Steps, Seyfried voices the character of Cinderella, a fairytale princess whose blue ballgowns and glass slippers have practically become engrained in the cultural consciousness. However, instead of opting for a more classic princess look, it seems Seyfried is choosing to embrace a more modern, cropped, and history-laden uniform, instead.

#6756. How New York and L.A. Celebrated Diwali in Style

Diwali—which translates to “festival of lights”—fêted by the global South Asian diaspora is a five-day celebration that began on Friday, November 6, a date decided by the Hindu lunar calendar. Diwali marks the new year, brings the promise of prosperity, and signifies the triumph of good over evil. While customs range across religion and region, the festival often means dedicating hours to baking sweets and lighting an unfathomable number of tea light candles, as well as giving up meat, fish, and alcohol. There’s also the deep cleaning rituals—to make room for blessings.

But in the U.S., more epicurean customs have emerged, which means weeks of parties, dinners, and gatherings in the lead-up. It’s proving to be a loophole for more indulgent fanfare before the official start of Diwali. Here’s Vogue’s look inside the celebrations everyone was talking about this year.

“Look around, look out the windows: We’re in New York City,” Jessel Taank told the crowd gathered at Boom at the Standard High Line. For the ŌUSHQ founder and Real Housewives of New York star, this soirée was one she had been dreaming of for some time. “On January 1st I wrote in my little notebook, ‘Host Diwali at The Standard’ as it was something I really wanted to do,” she said. “Growing up, Diwali was more of an intimate, community thing and what it’s become is so extraordinary.”

For the second annual Diwali Noir party presented by the fashion platform in partnership with the Council of Fashion Designers of America, Taank was joined on hosting duty by Prakti Beauty founder and model Pritika Swarup and the CFDA’s Marc Karimzadeh.

The high-octane evening invited guests to embrace an “Indian-inspired” dress code. “We really wanted to crush the stereotypes, because when you think of Indian fashion it is really occasionwear-heavy, big lehenga cupcakes, and embellishments,” Taank told Vogue. “I don't think Indian fashion is like that anymore. There’s a lot of creative energy coming from the Middle East and India that doesn’t get enough credit and recognition.”

Taank wore a metallic and bejeweled chocolate gown by Prabal Gurung, while Swarup opted for a bright punch-pink floor-length Rahul Mishra dress. “Look at everyone here tonight,” Swarup chimed in. “We wanted them to have their own interpretation of what modern Indian fashion is—and everyone looks incredible.”

Jenna Lyons donned sunglasses and an all-black ensemble topped with a bow, designer Sami Miro adorned herself in jewels from luxury Indian brand Outhouse, and mother-daughter duo Rachel Roy and Ava Dash took traditional Indian garments—palazzo pants and baroque blouses—and played with silhouettes, adding plumes of crimson fur and a flash of midriff.

While Diwali was the reason for the celebration, the night itself felt like an exercise in cultural exchange and discovery. Guests included Daniel Boulud, Bibhu Mohapatra, Kate Davidson Hudson, Katya Tolstova, Madhulika Sharma, Ankur Jain, Carly Cushnie, Ronny Kobo, Michelle Ochs, Roopal Patel, Dhaval Bhanusali, Azeezah Khan, Natalie De’Banco, Priya Shukla, Jay Sean, Akbar Hamid, and Junaid Mahmood, alongside Taank’s fellow cast members Sai De Silva, Erika Hammond, and Devyn Simone.

The evening also marked the official re-launch of ŌUSHQ’s multi-brand e-commerce website and the introduction of its new editorial destination dedicated to fashion, culture, and designer discovery. Behind the bar, towers of Johnnie Walker Blue Label bottles spiraled towards the ceiling as bartenders whipped up martinis, margaritas, and poured countless glasses of Champagne. Hammond and De Silva sipped cocktails and giggled with Miro, while stylist Micaela Erlanger perched at the end of the bar with Natasha Das, founder of Danarys, who nibbled on spicy bites of lamb, and morsels like samosas and pakora. “Diwali is quickly becoming one of my favorite party seasons,” Erlanger quipped.

On the other side of the room, the dance floor heaved, as Bollywood favorites like the 1999 hit “Dilbar” blended with Afro tech, while the Egyptian hit “Ah Ya Albi” played alongside Keinemusik’s “Move.” The music paused once briefly to give way to dancers who, atop the bar, performed a routine that, much like the dress code, blended India and the West.

“Can I just say, I don’t remember the last time I was in a room with so many beautiful people and so many beautifully dressed people,” added Karimzadeh, senior director of content and communications at the CFDA. “This is amazing.”

As speeches concluded, the party loosened further, turning from a bustling soiree to an all-out “rager”—to quote Taank. EDM and hip-hop boomed through the speakers, drinks spilled, dresses were trampled on, and by 1 a.m. the Champagne eventually ran out.

“We take for granted that the journey from gas to dust to protostar to star to supernova takes more than just a miracle—it takes time,” Gold House executive chairman and CEO Bing Chen shared in his remarks at The Majestic Downtown. It was a fitting metaphor for what Gold House called its largest Gold Diwali yet.

The organization threw its celebration for the Festival of Lights in Los Angeles, marking both its expansion as an institution and Diwali’s growing relevance. “Diwali is a celebration of light, community, and connection, and we wanted to bring that spirit to our Gold Diwali while honoring how culture shapes who we are and the possibilities we create,” Chen said.

The event began with the cast and producers of Ramayana: Part 1: Rise of a Legend introducing themselves and the film, released on November 5, which has already grossed over $56 million at the box office. It is also the most expensive film to be made in the region.

Gold House met the moment and announced a new partnership with nonprofit film fund South Stack Studios to launch the Gold Stack Shorts Fund, supporting short films and micro-series focused on South Asian stories.

The crowd, which was a bustling gathering of prominent entertainers, CEOs, and creators, brought together the likes of Freida Pinto, Tan France, Hannah Simone, Avantika, Dhar Mann, Richa Moorjani, and Rhea Raj, as well as Blumhouse president Abhijay Prakash, Poshmark founder Manish Chandra, and Anita Chatterjee.

Many attendees stuck to tradition, with jewel-toned lehengas, statement jewelry, saris, and bright sherwanis, but some played around with patent corsets in place of blouses and mini skirts.

Around the room, orange and golden marigolds were arranged in big, lush clusters with tropical palm fronds and brass lanterns. Friends, old and new, came together and enjoyed Diwali customs: Some grazed on a South Asian menu by Rasoi Catering, many danced as DJ MissNINJA performed with a live tabla performance, and others congregated in a dedicated Carrom Game Lounge where they played the traditional board game.

Indian luxury designer Anita Dongre debuted a one-off carrom board, painted by hand in collaboration with Gold House, that recontextualizes the tabletop game as a contemporary design object. Also on display was the Cuyana x Gold House Marigold Charm, a limited-edition piece released earlier in October.

Indian fashion house Sabyasachi’s multi-year collaboration with The Metropolitan Museum culminated in his first New York show in almost 20 years. So hosting the first Diwali party of its kind inside the hallowed halls of the storied institution, in many ways, felt fated.

“Ever since New York started having an official Diwali calendar, I wanted to host a party—and what could be a better venue than this,” designer Sabyasachi Mukherjee told Vogue. “It’s so iconic and it’s so New York. I think people are excited about this, so I’m very honored.”

Inside the American Wing’s Charles Engelhard Court, a crowd gathered to show off their opulent garments, from sleek sherwanis and richly textured shalwar kameez to sequined dresses and sharply tailored suits. Close friends of the designer, like Anjula Acharia, Jessel Taank, and Micaela Erlanger, all wore head-to-toe Sabyasachi looks, right down to the jewelry.

Guests in attendance included Kal Penn, Amy Fine Collins, Fern Mallis, Rhea Raj, Romilly Newman, Alioune Badara Fall, Nell Rebowe, Shruti Ganguly, Marie Ecot, Merritt Beck, Linda Fargo, Isiah Magsino, Imran Amed, Yumi Shin, Jully Patel, Angelica Hicks, and Carlos Mota.

As a six-piece band rattled off sultry renditions of songs like Dean Martin’s “Sway,” attendees were greeted with silver trays of Dom Pérignon Champagne and Petrossian caviar. Though most ended up mesmerized by what stood in the center of the room: A spectacular 16-foot-long grazing table, which was more like a culinary cornucopia outfitted with a peacock and an astounding bloom of ranunculus, roses, peonies, and winterberries. On offer, towering croquembouches, meringues, decadent cakes, and overflowing displays of fine chocolates and Indian sweets were placed alongside a lavish raw bar of fresh Maine lobster and oysters, fine Iberico ham, and endless types of cheese.

As Bollywood actress Rani Mukerji and designer Waris Ahluwalia eagerly posed for photos with Sabyasachi, excited brides-to-be lined up to introduce themselves to the designer, brimming with equal parts awe and nerves. Other guests sipped on spiced margaritas—which seems to be the emerging signature cocktail of the Diwali season—and lounged by the fountains.

Once the drinks dwindled and the band packed up, guests slowly made their way outside, reluctant to end the glamorous night. As everyone spilled out onto the iconic Met steps, a few who glittered even in the darkness of the crisp fall night beckoned for one more photo. For some, this was just another swanky party in Manhattan, but for those who grew up celebrating Diwali, it was a night for the history books.

Buzzy Indian restaurant the Ambassador’s Clubhouse turned Manhattan’s NoMad into a vibrant hub of revelry, as Anjula Acharia welcomed an exclusive guest list to her glitzy annual black-tie ball. “So many of you didn’t get plus ones,” she quipped over the mic. “So it means that all of you have to talk to everybody.”

The beloved All That Glitters Diwali Ball once again celebrated South Asian excellence, presented in partnership with Lexus. Guests in attendance included Avantika Vandanapu, Jay Sean, Rhea Raj, Bela Bajaria, Jessel Taank, Aasif Mandvi, Poorna Jagannathan, Mira Nair, Amrit Kaur, Nimesh Patel, Sheena Melwani, designers Falguni and Shane Peacock, and Revolve’s Divya Mathur.

“Tonight is my love letter to New York and all the South Asians here that are rising and thriving,” Acharia said. “So many of you have been grinding for decades. This is a celebration of all the work that you do for our community and for yourselves. I’m just so proud to honor all of you and I really mean that from the bottom of my heart.”

New York’s sudden cold snap was no match for the glamour that was put on show. Outside, some braved the cold for a Rhudeva scent station that offered engraved bottles of perfumes, including Dusky Diwali with notes of saffron, salted pistachio, and sandalwood. Inside, the room was a smorgasbord of crimson, as red flowers layered every surface from floor to ceiling.

As guests cozied up, sipping on piquant negronis, lassi-flavored cocktails, and martinis, bright plates of Punjabi food were passed around. Think: Wagyu-infused naan and lamb curry to samosas and spiced bites of goat. Subtlety was not on the menu, nor was it the dress code. Feathers trailed behind glittery saris, sequins caught the candlelight, and silk pooled and swished, while jhumkas and bangles clinked as Calvin Harris, Burna Boy, Charli XCX, and Vishal Dadlani boomed through the speakers.

“This is a far cry from the Diwaliis that I used to host myself, 20 or 30 years ago on Riverside Drive,” filmmaker Mira Nair told the crowd. “We are all here to be counted for, to be seen, and to be actually celebrating ourselves and our amazing community, that finally is visible in the most powerful of ways.”

East met West, as Jagannathan opted for South Asian designer Rahul Mishra in an untraditional rendition of desi opulence. Taank took a more modern route, and revealed her back tattoo with a pearlescent Tarun Tahiliani halter gown, while actress Avantika stuck with tradition in a warm copper lehenga and clutched onto a Coach Tabby purse.

For everyone in attendance, more was, well, more. Acharia floated across the room in a gilded silver Falguni Shane Peacock train adorned with feather cuffs, and Raj also tapped the designer for a custom magenta feathered two-piece that felt fitting for the rising pop star.

As the dance floor got warmed up (and subsequently didn’t stop until after 1 a.m.), Anita Chatterjee, founder of A-Game Public Relations, recalled: “Years ago, I remember being in Anjula’s Tribeca loft, where she put together a small Diwali party. Back then, she told me: ‘One day, everyone's gonna know about Diwali. There's going to be so many parties, and that’s what I want. I want our holiday and what we do to be seen by all.’ Anjula: mission accomplished. We did it!”

Passerine co-founders Maneesh K. Goyal and Alvina Patel Buxani shut down their Flatiron restaurant and set the scene for an early Diwali celebration with their second annual A Luminous Table dinner.

The gathering, which also raised funds for the Asian American Writers’ Workshop, was co-hosted by filmmaker Mira Nair, journalist Radhika Jones, and novelist Salman Rushdie.

A crowd from across fashion, finance, politics, and art convened, including Tamron Hall, Aasif Mandvi and B.D. Wong, Bibhu Mohapatra, Waris Ahluwalia, Alok Vaid-Menon, and June Ambrose, who eschewed her signature statement hat for sparkles and silk.

In true desi style, guests wore bright splashes of color, embellished lehengas, and luxurious saris, filling the air with soft metallic pops of bangles and jhumkas. Those without traditional outfits reveled in color, sparkles, and sequins. After all, it’s one of the few times all-black is considered a faux pas in New York City.

After a cocktail reception with plenty of Moët Hennessy on offer, a family-style dinner was served by executive Chef Gaurav Bathla. Guests took their seats at tables laden with bud vases of tulips, hyacinths, and carnations and quickly made introductions. Ambrose shook hands with Zara Rahim, Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s senior advisor, Rushdie and Italian artist Francesco Clemente chatted over red wine, and art curator Racquel Chevremont and her fiancé Mel Corpus made fast friends with their seat mates.

Siblings and friends were purposefully separated, as were some couples. “I created the seating chart that way intentionally,” Buxani told Vogue. “I wanted to create new friends so I separated some old ones. I think I have a good idea of who would get along.”

The food forged connections too. Starters like Goan chicken cafreal, Tamil shrimp Chettinad, and a samosa in Levantine katafi were quickly devoured, followed by baskets of naan and rice and a short rib pot pie filled with Old Delhi nihari, plumes of steam escaping from under its laminated pastry when theatrically cracked into.

Community was the guiding principle of the night, as co-hosts shared their stories of how Diwali offered respite as they navigated identity, immigration, and religion.

“When I was growing up in Bombay, the festivals were for all of us. It didn’t matter if we were Hindu, Muslim, Parsi—Diwali was ours,” Rushdie shared. “We all celebrated everything. And I think that this spirit is alive in this gathering.”

The celebrated novelist also noted that this energy is no longer part of the India he once knew.“There is something going on in India right now. India is boiling. And I would feel wrong not to say, maybe it’s not the thing to say in a restaurant, to celebrate the cockroach. But the young people of India have given us the most hopeful moment for a very long time.”

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is a propulsive Gen Z political movement in India that emerged earlier this year, using protests and demonstrations to demand government accountability, transparency, and major reforms across employment, education, and elections. Some have even referred to it as the Mamdani effect.

“I’m here as a mama cockroach,” Nair announced to the room to raucous cheers and applause, as the room swelled at the mention of her son, Zohran Mamdani. “Happy Diwali to all of us who believe in change. God knows the Cockroach Janta Party is reminding us that it is not enough to be quiet, it is not enough to celebrate, it is not enough to cease to question.” Her speech culminated in the room serenading her with a surprise birthday singalong.

As hot sticky date puddings covered in jaggery caramel filled the tables, Goyal stood for one last announcement. “In the old school tradition of people who live above their bodegas or restaurants, my husband and I, we live above this restaurant. There’s an after-hang at our apartment upstairs, and whether you come for 10 minutes or for two hours, everybody’s welcome. And let’s be honest, we’re New Yorkers. We like to see each other’s apartments!”

As the last sips of chili margaritas and tomato martinis were polished off, people slowly began heading for the door, and onwards to Goyal’s apartment for one more drink, one more story, and to make one more friend.

#6755. Another ‘Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Star Has Quietly Filed for Divorce, Per Court Documents

Just days after Jen Affleck filed for divorce from Zac Affleck, it looks like another Secret Lives of Mormon Wives cast member is officially pulling the plug on her marriage.

The Sun reports that Miranda Hope has filed for divorce from her estranged husband Chase McWhorter, news that comes a full two years after their separation. Per the outlet, which accessed court docs, she “opted to keep the filing and other documents related to the case private” but “a child support worksheet and a notice of required classes were also filed.”

Miranda and Chase got married in 2017, and they’ve had a lot of ups and downs navigating their split and coparenting their kids. It’s unclear what triggered Miranda to formally file for divorce after two years (note: she’s been referring to herself as “divorced” for some time now), but she’s moved on and is dating Kaleb Winterburn.

Back in July, Miranda spoke about her relationship with Chase to Page Six, saying, “It’s best case scenario for being divorced and coparenting. It’s not always seamless, we still argue and there’s ebbs and flows. I think that at the end of the day, something that Chase and I both pride ourselves on is the fact that we always put our kids first. So even when there are those ebbs and flows and those lows, our number one priority is the kids. Being able to have this type of relationship where we still have a family dynamic, we still consider ourselves and refer to ourselves as a family. We’re still a family, it just looks different. You have two homes.”

Miranda also added that she doesn’t have expectations for Chase as a partner, she just expects him to be a teammate: “Our relationship took a different form and we’re both so much better for it.”

#6753. Kate Middleton's “Cinnamon Bun” Chignon Is Her Most Regal Style Yet

The royal’s updo for the National Service of Remembrance ceremony was timeless and sophisticated

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It’s no surprise that many beauty lovers look to the royal family for quiet-luxury and glam inspiration. Yesterday, during the United Kingdom’s National Service of Remembrance ceremony at the Cenotaph in London, Princess Kate provided another reference point worth bookmarking: an oversized, off-center chignon.

Kate’s voluminous updo peeked out from under a wide-brimmed hat, gathered at the nape of her neck and pinned on the left-hand side. Paired with minimal makeup, including rosy cheeks, a coral lip, and her signature subtle smoky eye, Kate’s beauty styling exuded pure understated elegance. To get the look at home and minimize frizz, a few generous spritzes of hairspray, like L'Oréal Paris’ Elnett Extra Strong Hold, are key in locking the chignon in place.

While the royal is often touted for her loose, beachy waves, this distinguished look is a masterclass in traditional polished princess style. Arranged in layers, the princess’s sun-kissed highlights shone through even under the hat, complemented by her structured black coat by Catherine Walker, adorned with a red poppy brooch. And as evidenced by the tone of her still-bronde hair since she debuted the color courtside at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow last August, Kate doesn’t seem to be planning to transition to a darker shade any time soon.

#6750. Mocha Brown Hair-Color Season Is Here—and It’s Universally Flattering

There’s something about this time of year that makes everybody want to go darker. From their nail polish to their wardrobe, it’s a turn toward rich, darker shades. So it’s only natural that hair color would follow suit, going deeper and darker too. This winter in particular, it’s all about mocha brown.

Also called mocha chocolate, the rich, glossy shade was first popularized by celebrity colorist Jenna Perry, whose multidimensional brunette wizardry has fans like Bella Hadid and Kaia Gerber. Since then, the smooth and chocolaty hue—which combines darker espresso tones with lighter, milkier brunette shades—has become popular with a much wider section of the A-list, with Hailey Bieber and Daisy Edgar-Jones among the latest devotees.

“It reminds me of a chocolate mousse or a rich chocolate cake,” Perry tells Vogue. “That’s where the name came from. I thought mocha chocolate resembled the decadence of this shade of brown.” In line with sweater weather, Perry has churned out individualized takes on what she calls the “universally flattering brunette hair color” for a slew of stars, including longtime client Emily Ratajkowski and Amelia Gray. “A deep, rich brunette is chic,” Perry says. “The color reflects warmly in the sun, so it doesn’t ever look drab.”

According to Stephen Buller and Anita Rice, founders of Buller and Rice salon, these cacao tones feel luxurious for winter, particularly when the color isn’t completely flat. The key? Having a varied tone. “This is important throughout the lengths and ends so it reflects light and feels expensive rather than looking like one solid block of dark color,” they say. “This also gives clients who have had years of balayage an opportunity to go darker without feeling as though they’re simply covering everything up.”

Celebrity hairstylist Lorraine Dublin says that these indulgent, chocolaty shades look especially beautiful on textured and curly hair: “Think deep espresso brown with subtle ribbons of mocha, creating a rich, multidimensional finish,” she previously told Vogue. “It works beautifully on textured hair because the tonal variations catch the light, highlighting the shape and movement of curls, coils, and kinks.” She recommends asking your colorist for a “rich espresso base” with “delicate mocha or cinnamon brown accents,” which will impart a soft, seamless color melt.

Another important part of mastering the mocha chocolate look is keeping hair strong and shiny. “What makes this hair color so incredible from the start is having healthy hair,” explains Perry, who adds that preserving pigments with a color-safe shampoo and conditioner is key. Try Matrix Total Results Brass Off Shampoo to nix brassy or red tones. You can also use an at-home gloss or color conditioner, like Glaze Supergloss Color Conditioning Hair Gloss Chocolate Gleam or John Frieda Brilliant Brunette Color Vibrancy Conditioner, to prolong your hair’s vibrancy.

If a rich shade of mocha chocolate sounds like a delectable prospect, discover even more mocha brown hair-color inspiration to take to your salon below.

#6748. Rihanna Completes Her Sporty Shopping Look With a Pair of Suede Sneaker Mules

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Rihanna is simply not on the same fashion playing field as the rest of us. Sure, she’s besties with some of the world’s biggest designers, and she has access to many of the latest collections before they even hit the stores, but she also just has an utterly sui generis approach to styling. In her universe, a burger run calls for a tiered, tiramisu-colored maxi dress and clerical errands are done in oversize, avant-garde suits. When it comes to tricks, like wearing a foulard as a skirt or treating an exposed-bra as a statement piece, she’s always at the head of the pack. Then, of course, there’s her maternity wear, which speaks quite loudly for itself.

So, it should come as no surprise that, even when she’s keeping things casual, Rihanna still manages to slip in a fabulous surprise or two. And on Sunday, that intriguing touch came courtesy of some hybrid footwear, which RiRi casually incorporated into her sporty off-duty look.

As she enjoyed a bit of nighttime shopping at the Grove in Los Angeles, the “Diamonds” singer bundled up in a baby-pink button-up and cocoa-colored slacks, which she layered underneath an ecru trench with a shiny golden lining.

Rihanna tied the coat loosely around her waist so as not to conceal the Neapolitan-colored outfit underneath, and she complemented her trench’s interior with a thick gold collar necklace. In her hand, she carried a monogrammed Speedy from Louis Vuitton, and she popped on a pair of chunky creamsicle-colored sunglasses from Saint Laurent.

But it was the most nondescript element that turned out to be the most striking. To match her coat, the singer and business mogul slipped into a pair of buff-colored suede sneakers from the New Balance x Miu Miu collaboration, which were first unveiled back in 2024. However, these hybrid shoes weren’t actually sneakers at all, but rather mules, giving new shape to the classic New Balance 530 SL silhouette that they were inspired by.

And this is just the latest evidence of the ongoing designer deconstruction of the shoe. At Chanel, Matthieu Blazy is offering up sandals that only cover the wearer’s heels. At Saint Laurent, Anthony Vaccarello presented Oxfords made out of see-through PVC.

Now, leave it to Rihanna to pull out the perfect transitional footwear for fall.

#6746. Ariana Grande Is Back in the Spotlight and Looking Chicer Than Ever

She made a surprise appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon to promote her upcoming movie

Ariana Grande is back! The superstar has been absent from the spotlight since she wrapped her Eternal Sunshine Tour on September 1, and stepped away from public roles and duties (including the West End revival of Sunday in the Park With George) due to harsh online scrutiny regarding her physical appearance.

But now, she’s bopping back onto the stage—even if that stage is a late-night show set rather than a concert arena.

Last night, Grande made her big comeback with a surprise appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. She joined the show alongside her Focker-in-Law costars Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller to promote the upcoming holiday comedy film (which comes out November 25).

The “Hate That I Made You Love Me” singer looked so chic as she glided onto the stage in a sharp suit from Givenchy by Sarah Burton (look 20 from the Spring/Summer 2027 collection). The double-breasted wool blazer was slightly oversize, and paired with matching cigarette pants.

Grande, styled by none other than Law Roach, kept the look sleek and monochromatic. The duo opted to pair the black suit with pointy suede heels and a velvet choker, while the musician’s little bob was curled upward at the ends for an extra sweet, classy touch.

The singer also brought some of her on-stage persona with her to the late-night show via her makeup, which was rosy and glittery, matching her glossy pink lip and powder-pink manicure. Tiny gold hoop earrings completed the look.

#6744. Inside Designer Carla Fernández’s Vibrant Mexico City Home, Full of Indigenous Textiles and Art

When the Mexico City–based writer and curator Su Wu started working on her new design book, a theme began to emerge: She kept noticing the presence of pre-Hispanic architectural and design traditions in modern Mexican interiors.

It was from this realization that Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes was born. The book features 16 homes across Mexico—those of artists, architects, designers, and more—all shot by photographer Luis Garvan.

Wrought iron doors designed by Carla Fernández.

“When I began this project, I thought that we would be documenting a history, like the aura surrounding the artifacts in a museum, the apparitions of the past,” Wu writes in the book’s introduction. “Instead, what I’ve found is the vibrant, living presence of Indigenous ideas in Mexico.”

“In the guest bedroom, pink silk curtains dyed by Fernández cast a glow in the room. The bedspread is from her personal collection of Mesoamerican textiles, made of undyed wool in Teotitlán del Valle, Oaxaca.”—Su Wu

One space that exemplifies those ideas is Casa Flora, the colorful brutalist Mérida home and studio of the Mexican fashion designer Carla Fernández. As a designer, Fernández seeks to preserve the textile traditions of Indigenous and Mestizo communities through collaborations with artisans, bringing ancient practices to a contemporary audience. Fittingly, the home is full of Mesoamerican art and textiles.

Fernández led the renovation of the house, which dates back more than a century and now hosts workshops for Taller Flora, her design lab, which focuses on traditional Indigenous clothing techniques. (You can also stay in the home; the designer lists it for stays on Airbnb.)

Fernández’s husband, the artist Pedro Reyes, created several elements of the space, including a concrete outdoor shower, as well as some of the tiles throughout the space. His sculptures—including a prototype of Mitla Sillas, chairs inspired by the pyramids of the Mitla archaeological site in Oaxaca—are found throughout the home.

The outdoor shower designed by Pedro Reyes.

Reflecting on Fernández’s home, Wu tells Vogue: “I was very moved when writing the book with the idea of the ‘void’ in Mesoamerican architecture, and how so many architects, going back to the writings of Teodoro González de León, described the patio as a central, defining feature of the Mesoamerican home, a space that is at once enclosed and open to the elements. And in Carla’s home, I think there are many moments that exemplify this idea of the boundary between interior and exterior being not a physical one, but rather a marker of movement across psychological states.”

“A latticed window, known in Mexico as a celosia, is a central part of Mesoamerican architecture, used for cross-ventilation and to create a permeable sense of separation and shadow.”—Su Wu

Prototypes of Reyes’s Mitla Sillas chairs.

For Wu, Casa Flora is also a prime example of an idea that chef Elena Reygadas wrote about in her foreword to the book, “which is that handmade things are meant to be lived with no matter how precious, or especially if precious.”

“An equipale chair made of bent wood by the Wixárika people in Nayarit sits in front of a backstrap-loom tapestry of the Torre Latinoamericana, the iconic skyscraper in Mexico City designed by architect Augusto H. Álvarez. Made by artisans from San Juan Cancuc, Chiapas, the tapestry echoes a collection of dresses from Carla Fernández that featured historic buildings in Mexico City.”—Su Wu

All images © Luis GarvanCasa Flora, Mérida, Yucatán (pages 244-263). Mesoamerican Modern: Ancient Ideas in Contemporary Mexican Homes by Su Wu. Published by Phaidon Press.

#6742. Sabrina Carpenter Would Love to Star in a 9 to 5 Movie Musical

The star talks Dolly Parton, the French New Wave, and her Johnnie Walker short with Damien Chazelle.

For Sabrina Carpenter, a song and a role each offer a different way into a story. “Acting and music have always gone hand in hand for me,” she tells ELLE exclusively. “With music, I get to tell stories through my own perspective, and with acting I get to step into someone else’s world and bring their story to life, and that is always an exhilarating feeling for me.”

Carpenter gets to move between those perspectives in a new Johnnie Walker film directed by Damien Chazelle, the Oscar-winning visionary behind Whiplash and La La Land. With the Short n’ Sweet star at its center, the clip nods to French New Wave cinema through the director’s signature motion-driven style.

The short begins with Carpenter, in a mod embellished minidress, stepping into an unusually quiet party. As someone pours her a Go Go Highball, her signature Johnnie Walker cocktail, the scene comes to life: the guests spring into motion, and Carpenter gets swept up in the revelry while a meta quartet of directors looks on. Here, she opens up to ELLE about working with Chazelle, her favorite New Wave films, and the movie musical she’d most want to star in (hint: it’s a certain blonde’s workplace comedy).

This past year has been pretty surreal. Coachella will always be a standout for me, probably for the rest of my life. I had so much fun creating that show. Also getting to perform onstage this year with Madonna and Stevie Nicks. [I’m] still processing that.

Sometimes the best moments are just spending time with the people you love, and this summer spending some downtime with my close friends and my sister, we loved our Go Go Highballs for sure.

Getting ready for my Met Gala after-party comes to mind. But I can’t always reveal all the details to you guys; there’s no fun in that.

Working with Damien was a dream! I’ve admired his work for so long, and he has a brilliant way of making even the smallest moments feel larger than life. I love how he was able to capture the humor and playfulness that come with life’s unexpected moments.

I love La La Land! I think there’s something really special about creating a short moment or scene that feels almost like a whole movie, so I’m always trying to approach these projects from a cinematic viewpoint.

Two of my favorites are The Umbrellas of Cherbourg and Cleo from 5 to 7.

Well, I just rewatched 9 to 5 and you know I’m the biggest Dolly [Parton] fan. So that would be a fun one.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6741. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6740. The Fall Winter 2026 Fashion Trends to Know and Shop Now

If recent seasons have been defined by understated dressing, the fall-winter 2026 trends mark a shift toward a more expressive approach to style. However, there’s still a piece of the cake for every aesthetic to cut into. Across the runways, designers embraced the art of contrast. By pairing clean, minimalist silhouettes with rich textures—and reimagining classic wardrobe staples with unexpected details like a peplum or a voluminous shape—they proved that practicality and personality can coexist. The result is a season that feels both wearable and exciting.

Leading the conversation this season are six standout trends that capture fashion’s evolving mood. The Updated Lady introduces a fresh take on suiting for the modern woman, complete with feminine touches and softened structures. (Take a look at Chanel, Balenciaga, and Jil Sander for fresh inspiration, for starters.) Elsewhere, collections at Khaite, Kallmeyer, and Conner Ives nodded to the golden age of the 1920s, incorporating elegant Art Deco touches throughout. An unexpected take on proportions has entered the chat, too, with Tory Burch and Celine reconfiguring preconceived notions of size and shape. Designers, from Prada to Loewe, leaned on the power of styling, too, showcasing how layering and a close attention to detail can transform a wardrobe. For a more alluring take on the season, Alaïa and Valentino celebrated the female form through body-hugging silhouettes and delicate sheer pieces. Meanwhile, Dries Van Noten and Erdem embraced the spirit of fall with down-to-earth palettes of green and brown, punctuated by dark floral patterns.

Discover a shoppable first look at the key fall winter 2026 fashion trends before they fully take over. Don’t forget to come back to this story for more.

Unlike past seasons, there wasn’t one definitive silhouette for tailoring this fall. Let’s start with suiting. Designers don’t want you to stay within the lines. Many jackets were shown with mismatched trousers and skirts; lapel linings were exposed; traditional collared shirts were left undone and wrinkled; collars were turned up and styled with one in and one out. Some blazers shrank; some went long and lean. Others were cropped, nipped in, or even made sculptural.

In autumn’s sea of black coats and navy sweaters, choose color. This season, designers made it simple, showing a slew of head-to-toe looks in vivid monochrome hues. Take your pick! The runways offered a spin around the contemporary color wheel with splashes of color-drenched leather bags and footwear. From knits to denim, dresses to outerwear, we can’t think of a reason not to try this kind of energetic dressing.

This isn’t your grandmother’s lace! On the fall runways, designers from Altuzarra and Colleen Allen to Bottega Veneta, Dior, and Gabriela Hearst embraced a more dramatic kind of romance, with cascading layers, frothy ruffles, and sheer, sweeping silhouettes. Get the look with a delicate lace blouse paired with a tiered black skirt, or go all in with a floor-length lace dress. The effect is romantic, but anything but prim.

Photos: Courtesy of Kallmeyer, Khaite, Rabanne, Chanel, and Loro Piana

Although F. Scott Fitzgerald’s 1925 novel, The Great Gatsby, predates the height of the design style, its themes of 1920s luxury have permanently associated the story with the movement’s signature geometric patterns and overt opulence. From Khaite to Colleen Allen, designers embraced the era with richly detailed texture, glamorous shapes, fringe, gloves, and velvet. To quote the iconic host himself: “Can’t repeat the past? Why, of course, you can!” For 2026, the era returns with a modern, streamlined touch—ready for daily wear to elegant soirées.

Photos: Courtesy of Chanel, Stella McCartney, Givenchy, Jil Sander, and Chloé

The fall-winter 2026 runways showcased a sense of whimsy through bold proportions, featuring oversized designs, cropped styles, and exaggerated silhouettes. Cocoon-like tailoring, dramatic hemlines, and billowy pants and dresses create an expressive and eye-catching approach to fashion. This trend embraces a bit of drama (because that’s life!) while also maintaining a sense of balance. Unconventional silhouettes might feel daunting to incorporate into your daily lineup, so start with small touches. Destree’s jacquard blouse balances voluminous shoulders with a fitted waist that pairs easily with jeans, while Aflalo’s tapered white balloon pants feel airy and light—just add a layered knit and coat for transitional dressing.

Photos: Courtesy of Ferragamo, Loewe, Prada, Johanna Parv, The Row (middle)

Primarily inspired by the fall/winter 2026 Prada runway, the power of styling was a reminder that great style isn’t about owning more—it’s about seeing familiar pieces, like cardigans and tailored trousers, in a new light. Everyday wardrobe staples were transformed through unique pairings, layered basics, and unexpected accessories to create ensembles that demand a second glance. Styling, too, becomes a vessel for self-expression, allowing you to make each piece your own through personal touches and a careful attention to detail.

Photos: Courtesy of Dior, Chanel, Givenchy, Balenciaga, Proenza Schouler, Kallmeyer

Current, confident, and sophisticated, the Updated Lady emerged as one of fall-winter 2026’s defining archetypes, with houses like Chanel, Givenchy, and Balenciaga reimagining power dressing through a contemporary lens. Rather than rigid corporate suiting, the season favored softened structures, explored through gently sloping waists, sculpted jackets, and rich textures that balance strength with ease. The modern woman is multifaceted and full of contradictions, balancing polish with her own distinct edge—shouldn’t her wardrobe follow suit?

Photos: Courtesy of Gucci, Gorunway.com, Khaite and Alaïa

Bodies, bodies, bodies! The fall 2026 runways were an homage to the female form. From the second-skin dresses at Alaïa—some of which actually walked in flesh-colored nude—to Khaite’s sheer layers and Valentino’s lingerie-inspired slips, little was left to the imagination. Translating the trend into your own fall rotation may seem far-fetched, but by embracing it piece by piece, you can achieve an alluring look without going full naked dressing. Imagine Jil Sander’s knit bustier top with a slim trouser, Gucci’s cut-out leggings grounded by a crisp white tee, or one of Saint Lauren’s lace mini dresses beneath a sharp tailored blazer. To bring it back to one of the season’s strongest show notes—and one we outlined above: It all comes down to the styling.

It’s not unusual for fall trends to find inspiration in the countryside—whether it’s heritage plaids, khaki barn jackets, or some kind of cozy knit variation. As grounding as the source material may be, this season’s expression is more elaborate than ever. Nowhere is that more apparent than in the floral prints peppered throughout the collections: they’re richer, deeper, and even moodier than in years’ past. Par for the course, intricate floral brocades appeared at Dries Van Noten on everything from outerwear to midiskirts. Simone Rocha and Erdem also showcased their fair share of flora and fauna, from draped dresses to blouses, proving that the look can move between moods and occasions.

#6735. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.
