#6733. In ‘Possible Love,’ Jeon Do-yeon Delivers the Year’s Most Shattering Performance. Can It Take Her to the Oscars?

In the nearly three decades since she made her big-screen debut in 1997’s The Contact, Jeon Do-yeon has earned a richly deserved reputation in South Korea—and far beyond it—as the kind of actor who inhabits her characters so fully that it ceases to feel like acting at all. (International audiences likely know her best for 2007’s Secret Sunshine, a wrenching portrait of a grieving mother that made her the first Korean performer to win an acting prize at the Cannes Film Festival.)

Critics often reach for the word “fearless” to describe her, but when we speak via Zoom at the tail end of a marathon press day in Seoul, Jeon waves that notion away.

“I’m always scared, and I’m full of fear, especially in front of the camera,” she says, with a laugh. “I’ve been working as an actor for quite some time, but it’s an ongoing process.” In fact, it’s important to her that she never gets too comfortable. “I actually enjoy having that fear and anxiety, and trying my best to work through it, because sometimes something completely new comes out of that struggle.”

That willingness to sit in discomfort is vividly, devastatingly evident in Possible Love, out now on Netflix after a theatrical run in October—and recently selected as South Korea’s official submission for the 2027 Academy Awards. The film marks the long-awaited return of legendary auteur Lee Chang-dong (arguably best known for the hypnotic 2018 masterpiece Burning, which became the first Korean movie ever shortlisted for the best international feature Oscar and topped critics’ year-end lists across the West) after an eight-year hiatus, and a reunion for Jeon and Lee nearly 20 years after Secret Sunshine.

Constructed with Lee’s signature novelistic sweep, Possible Love centers on the complicated dynamic between two married couples from starkly different strata of contemporary Korean society. Jeon stars as Mi-ok, a pragmatic mask-factory worker living quietly with her young son and her husband, Ho-seok (played by her frequent screen partner Sul Kyung-gu). Years after a mass factory layoff and a violently suppressed labor strike, Ho-seok remains haunted by the trauma. When the funeral of a former co-worker brings them into the orbit of Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, best known as the rich mom in Parasite), an intellectual documentary filmmaker chronicling laid-off laborers, and her wealthy, enigmatic husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), Mi-ok agrees to let Ye-ji film their daily lives. Yet what begins as a study of liberal empathy—and a moving portrait of across-the-divide solidarity—gradually warps into something far more strange and ambiguous, exploring the fault lines of privilege, hidden desire, and voyeurism.

Oscar buzz has swirled around her performance—a stunning and powerfully subtle tightrope walk of stoicism and simmering longing—since the film premiered at the Venice Film Festival in September, but Jeon remains pragmatic about what all this fanfare actually means. “When I won the award at Cannes 20 years ago, I remember thinking, Is this going to change my life? Probably not. Am I going to change as an actor because I have a Cannes award?” she reflects. “I’m very happy that we’re competing at the Oscars, and it’s wonderful that people are talking about the film, but I don’t think it will change me or the way I perform in any way.”

Below, Jeon discusses her on-screen reunion with Sul Kyung-gu, the unlikely magic fostered by Lee Chang-dong’s aversion to having his actors rehearse, and how a story of trauma and class tension deeply rooted in Korean society found universal resonance.

Vogue: Now that Possible Love is streaming on Netflix and reaching a massive global audience, how are you feeling? Have you been hearing much feedback?

Jeon Do-yeon: I watched the movie once again as soon as it was on Netflix. I think Possible Love is a type of movie that leaves a different afterglow for different people, and people can analyze it differently and interpret it in endless ways. Now that it’s on Netflix, I feel like people are finding their own ways to think about the movie—it leaves a lot of food for thought. I’m very proud that people are talking a lot about it.

To go back to the beginning, you obviously have a deep history with director Lee Chang-dong. How did he first approach you about Possible Love? I believe this idea had been gestating for almost a decade.

I do know that Director Lee worked on this project for quite a long time—he had it in his mind for more than 10 years. Ten years ago, he wanted to talk about this worker and his wife, the couple who had been laid off. Sometimes that story diverged into different paths, and sometimes they were scrapped; I know there were a lot of different versions along the way. When I knew that he finally had a script, I really wanted to know what it was about. I was waiting for that script. [Laughs.]

Given how layered the story is, what struck you most when you finally read it? What drew you to Mi-ok?

When I first read the script, I could feel the 10 years’ worth of thought and effort that Director Lee put into it. I was very touched reading it, and I was like, “Of course this is a Chang-dong film. It is this good.” And then I thought about what I could relate to about my character, Mi-ok. Of all the traits that she has, I think she holds this anxiety, and that anxiety stems from her wish to protect certain things. Although Mi-ok may seem a little bit fragile or weak from the outside, I think she’s a very strong woman inside, so that is something that I took note of.

Zo In-sung as Sang-woo, Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok, and director Lee Chang-dong on the set of Possible Love.

One of the aspects of your performance I found most striking is the physicality—the way Mi-ok holds herself is such an important part of how her story is told. Did you develop that beforehand, or did you find it on set?

If I hadn’t worked with Director Lee before, then I would have spent a lot of time trying to learn more about this character and to deeply understand her. But I know how he works, and he always stresses emptying my mind as an actor. He wants me not to express, but to feel the character. The preparation process for me was mostly about making sure that I get very accustomed to the lines that my character speaks, so it really feels like it’s me speaking, but it’s actually Mi-ok speaking through me.

You’ve worked with Sul Kyung-gu more than any other actor in your career, I believe. So much of the film relies on the subtleties of that relationship—did your real-life friendship and trust help?

I think I really know him well in real life, and as an actor as well. But while we were working on this project, and as he transformed into the character of Ho-seok, I discovered new facets of him. There’s always a new side of him that would surprise me, so I’m still looking forward to working with him on another project so I can discover yet another new side of him. We have this friendship and trust that we’ve built over the years, and I’m pretty sure that they helped. When you’re trying to express the chemistry of a very long relationship of a married couple, sometimes you have to make efforts to show that aspect. But we didn’t have to try too hard because we already had that trust built between us. If we do look like a real married couple in the movie, I think it’s partly thanks to that.

Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok and Sul Kyung-gu as Ho-seok.

At the opposite end of the spectrum, this was your first time working with Cho Yeo-jeong. The dynamic between Mi-ok and Ye-ji walks a very delicate line between sisterhood and something more transactional. Did the two of you discuss that, or did you prefer to discover it in the room?

We actually didn’t talk about our characters before going into production. When you work with Director Lee, he’s sort of against the actors having too many biases or prejudices or information about characters before going into the shoot, because he believes something very novel and fresh can come out when it’s your first time being in that scene, when it’s your first time talking. I didn’t want to jinx that by speaking with her about our characters beforehand. In the beginning, my character, Mi-ok, believes that if Ye-ji films us, then that is a way of protecting my family—a way of finding hope. But as they get closer, she realizes that there is a gap between the two people, herself and Ye-ji, and the wall grows higher and higher as they get closer.

Director Lee is known for his naturalism. Did that mean doing dozens of takes until you lost the sense that you’re acting? Did scenes ever head in unexpected directions based on how you were all interacting?

Director Lee is not actually the type who shoots a lot of takes, because he doesn’t really tell us exactly what it is that he wants from a scene. What he tries to do instead is to look into the chemistry and the conversation between the actors and try to find something new from it. Instead of Director Lee saying, “Okay, let’s do the lines,” he would just say, “Why don’t we talk? Let’s talk.” He likes everything very lively and raw, so that’s how we did it, and he didn’t want us to have a lot of rehearsals. And regarding whether the direction of a scene actually changed after working—it didn’t happen, because there was no fixed direction in the beginning.

Jeon Do-yeon as Mi-ok and Cho Yeo-jeong as Ye-ji.

Korean cinema has obviously exploded in popularity globally over the past decade, and Possible Love is getting a huge amount of international attention. How do you view this global wave? Do you think much about reaching Western audiences?

I don’t have plans on “going global” or anything as an actor! But I do hope that Korean content and Korean cinema will be beloved around the globe going forward as well. It’s just such a joy to be able to share different stories and different emotions with people that speak different languages and have different cultures. It’s such a good opportunity for us to transcend borders, transcend language. I hope more of those opportunities will come.

Possible Love is rooted in a very specific Korean tragedy, yet the hollowing out of industrial working-class communities is something people recognize all over the world. Did you worry at all during filming about whether such a locally specific story would translate, especially on a global platform like Netflix?

When we were filming, we actually did think about how this is a very Korea-specific sort of incident. Would people around the world be able to resonate with this story? Particularly because there is no dramatic event that happens throughout the movie; it’s just about the four people and their emotions, and that’s what really brings a narrative towards the end. We were a little bit worried. But I actually realized after screening overseas that the issue of laid-off workers is not something that’s specific to Korea—it’s happening all around the world, and it is still happening in some parts of the world. I could feel that a lot of people who are not Korean, who don’t live in Korea, are resonating with the themes and the emotions that are captured in the movie. And the moon at the very end of the movie? Anybody in any part of the world can see the moon. That’s something that’s very universal.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

#6731. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6729. How Creative Director Hype Is Lifting Resale

Hype around new creative directors’ hit pieces — from Matthieu Blazy’s pony hair heels for Chanel to Michael Rider’s massive Celine Disc sunglasses — is having a halo effect on the resale market that’s rippling across eras and raising prices on key items.

That’s according to Ebay’s latest Watchlist report, which goes live today and takes stock of the rising resale trends for Fall/Winter 2026. The report sheds light on how creative debuts over the past year are impacting what and who people are searching for and selling, and how far the hype is extending beyond current collections.

Searches for Matthieu Blazy, for instance, jumped 291% when his first Chanel collection hit stores. At the same time, listings for Karl Lagerfeld-era Chanel rose 87% year-on-year. Searches for Demna rose 42% following his first Gucci runway show, while listings for Tom Ford-era Gucci increased 49% year-on-year, reflecting how users capitalize on current interest to sell past collections. It follows the trend of pieces from defining designer eras increasingly entering circulation on Ebay, from Demna’s Balenciaga (up 204% year-on-year) to Phoebe Philo’s Chloé (up 165%).

At Dior, meanwhile, searches for Jonathan Anderson rose 92% following his first couture show. Average sales prices for John Galliano-era Dior, meanwhile, increased 81% in the same period.

It’s a shift reflected across the resale market. Blazy’s appointment drove searches for the designer up 10,976% on The RealReal, according to The RealReal’s 2026 resale report, released in August, reflecting the impact current brand heat can have on its past collections circulating in the secondhand market. On Ebay, Chanel didn’t rank among the top-purchased luxury brands from 2022 to 2024. In 2025, it snagged fifth place, and in 2026, it jumped to third, trailing Louis Vuitton and Gucci (which have held the top two spots since 2022).

“When someone new takes the helm, they’re not necessarily reinventing the wheel but very often revisiting the codes, silhouettes and references that made the house interesting in the first place,” says stylist Brie Welch, who worked on the report as Ebay’s resident stylist. “Seeing a brand reinterpreted through a new creative lens naturally sparks curiosity about its past collections.”

It’s a sign of where consumers are at. Shoppers are following brands and their runway shows closely — evidenced by their inclination towards ultra-specific fashion search terms and the impact of a debut show on searches, listings, and sales. That consumers are turning to secondhand marketplaces like Ebay is indicative of shoppers’ desires to tap into current trends while finding better value. It’s reflective of trends in the primary marketplace: spending isn’t expected to dip, but consumers are placing greater emphasis on perceived value. If shoppers determine that this is better in the secondary marketplace than the primary, brands ought to pay attention.

Galliano’s Dior isn’t the only category seeing a price hike. Cultural heat has driven luxury secondhand prices up across the board, per Ebay’s findings. However, the fact that luxury prices continue to tick up has likely also played a role in the spike. Still, Kirsty Keoghan, Ebay’s general manager of EU fashion and luxury, credits many of the price increases (measured for this report from January to September 2026) to celebrity sightings.

The Row’s Margaux Bag, for instance, continues to climb in price, up 137% year-on-year. Celebs including Zoë Kravitz and Kendall Jenner sported the bag during this timeframe. Demand for Gucci’s Giglio tote, carried by Dakota Johnson and Suki Waterhouse, was up 103%.

“There is an intentionality about owning something with cultural relevance, longevity, and a sense of value,” Keoghan says, noting that shopping for secondhand designer fashion has become more culturally responsive.

This ties into the return of the It-bag, as shoppers look for styles they’re seeing blow up in culture. Global listings for Balenciaga’s Le City bag, which is having yet another resurgence, are up 936%. (Who could forget Sienna Miller getting papped in a denim mini skirt with her red city bag slung over her shoulder back in 2004? Now, the bag — which had its 25th anniversary on Monday — is on the arm of everyone from Harris Dickinson to Bella Hadid.) The Loewe Amazona 180 (up 440%), the Valentino Garavani VLogo Bag (up 358%), and the Bottega Veneta Veneta Bag (up 158%) are also seeing surges in listings, which Welch puts down to celeb style mainstays such as Kravitz and Jacob Elordi getting papped wearing and styling such bags.

Current runway trends are also feeding back into secondhand market purchases, as consumers seek to tap into what’s trending now via previous season pieces. At a moment when consumer anxiety is still high — which isn’t necessarily putting a dent on spending — opting for a pre-loved item when making a purchase as a style choice can feel like a safer bet versus a brand-new splurge, even as resale prices hike with demand, Keoghan says.

“We are seeing how quickly a new runway moment can evoke an interest for shoppers in a brand’s archive, sending them in search of special pieces with a story,” Keoghan says.

Prada skirts were a breakout trend not just in fashion discourse. Seemingly inspired by the show, shoppers turned to the secondhand market to source past collection skirts in the days following Prada’s SS27 show on September 22 in Milan. Global searches for “Prada skirt” spiked more than 360% compared to the beginning of September, reflecting a runway-inspired uptick.

“Suddenly, you’re looking at a sort of dated silhouette differently,” Welch says, noting that consumers are finding success looking at the secondhand marketplace for A-line skirts that exist in the market. “You can find an earlier version of the idea, sometimes at a more accessible price point, and make it your own.”

This season’s emphasis on shoes was also a search booster for resale. On Ebay, Chanel — which has had a heavy rotation of slingbacks on recent runways — seemed to have the biggest impact once again. Searches for slingbacks are up over 65% versus the start as fashion month, and searches for Chanel slingbacks are up 50%.

“People are shopping with a sharper point of view; they want to be part of the conversation, and they are shopping pre-loved to achieve that,” Keoghan says.

#6728. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6727. Should You Put Your Stem Cells in the Bank?

High-yield savings vs. a bad beauty and wellness investment.

As part of the Future of Beauty Awards, the ELLE beauty team looked ahead at what will be next in beauty and wellness.

Recently, I was at a dinner with fellow journalists where the small talk turned from the mysteriously pierced earlobes in The Odyssey and the best facialists in New York to banking. Seoul, one person chirped, is where all the innovation happens. A woman said that she had banked hers years ago in Texas. Then another person said he had heard that Japan was the country with some of the best facilities. A personal finance TikToker, who had written several books about saving money, leaned over and curiously asked, “Why are you guys banking in other countries instead of the US or Switzerland?” “Not money,” I clarified. “Stem cells.”

Humans have long squirreled away things of value, but it’s only recently that hoarding your stem cells—the building blocks of tissues and organs that have the ability to renew and become other cells—has become dinner conversation. Stem cells diminish over time as we age, but much like with money, there are a few ways to save young cells for a rainy day. Parents can bank their baby’s cord blood, a bit like starting a 529 education plan for college tuition. (They can also donate cord blood to a public bank for free, to help anyone who might need a stem cell transplant.) For those interested in beauty, there’s hope that preserving young stem cells from fat might give you a nice supply of growth factors that could keep your skin bouncy later. And then for a cohort of celebrities like John Cleese, Chris Hemsworth, and biohacker Bryan Johnson, there’s the belief that stem cell banking could be a well from which youth, cryopreserved, springs eternal. It’s like heavily investing in a call option you hope will pan out later. After visiting a clinic in Panama, Hemsworth posted on Instagram: “With this kind of technology available, I plan to keep making films well into my 100s (or 1,500 in Asgard).”

The discourse around stem cells, according to several experts, ranges from “tremendous” and “promising” to “wildly outrageous,” “misleading,” “harmless nonsense,” and “potentially very dangerous.” “The phrase stem cells has almost become a health halo,” says Timothy Caulfield, professor at the Faculty of Law and the School of Public Health and research director of the Health Law Institute at the University of Alberta. To understand the buzz, you have to go back to 2012, when Shinya Yamanaka, MD, PhD, co-won a Nobel Prize with John B. Gurdon for discovering that you can take mature cells and turn them back into an embryonic state. They called these new, artificially created stem cells induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells. Two decades later, Yamanaka’s findings are now being cautiously used on humans. In March 2026, iPS cell therapies were given conditional and time-limited marketing approval for seven years in Japan for heart failure and Parkinson’s disease, while studies continue to determine their efficacy and safety in clinical trials. In the U.S. in May, a patient received iPS cells in a clinical trial to study treatment of retinitis pigmentosa.

“Stem cells don’t do magic. They do biology,” cautions John O’Neill, PhD, cofounder of Sweet Chemistry and chief scientific officer of Xylyx Bio, Inc., a regenerative medicine company. “They may be capable of incredible, remarkable, and profound therapeutic benefits. But truly understanding, controlling, manufacturing, and scaling [stem cell usage] will take years and years and bazillions of dollars and an incredible amount of human power.” Aside from the conditional exceptions in Japan for treating heart failure and Parkinson’s disease, iPS cells are not available for medical use, clarifies Knut Woltjen, Dior Reverse Aging board member and associate professor at Kyoto University’s Center for iPS Cell Research and Application (the same center that Yamanaka helped create and direct in Japan). He says they “are primarily a research material.”

Nevertheless, do even a cursory Google search and you’ll find people proclaiming that some type of stem cell treatment “worked wonders.” In many cases, it’s uncertain where these stem cells are being sourced from. But some experts are skeptical that these treatments always involve the real thing. Caulfield calls it an “exploitative industry,” saying that “it’s gotten so bad that if you see the phrase ‘stem cells,’ I think that is a red flag for bunk.”

Even if people were receiving real stem cells, those cells can only do so much; many of the treatments marketed as such or as regenerative therapies have not undergone clinical testing to determine their safety and effectiveness, and it would likely take time before they become widely available for use in a nonmedical setting. “Today, the timing of marketing is quicker than scientific or research timing,” says Virginie Couturaud, Christian Dior Parfums scientific communication director.

The banks and places that collect, store, and process them are regulated by the FDA. Still, some states have their own specific licensing, inspection, and oversight requirements that prompt experts to ask, “If you bank your own stem cells, can they be used? Because it won’t necessarily fit into the regulatory environment,” says Robin Smith, MD, a partner at Exoceuticals, an exosome-based skin care brand. Federally, stem cell products that are used as medical treatments need the FDA’s approval and are regulated by the FDA, although Smith notes that several states have carved out exceptions for indications such as pain, wound healing, or orthopedics. In July, Wyoming enacted the Stem Cell Freedom Act, which allows physicians to administer certain non-FDA-approved therapies using a patient’s own stem cells and prohibits medical board sanctions. Wyoming State Senator Eric Barlow told local press: “We’ve got to press on the federal government because they’re not approving things fast enough.”

There is also the concern that because stem cells are so powerful, using your own could carry markers of the very same diseases or ailments that you are trying to treat. “They have so much potency and ability, they could become the wrong thing in the body and get the wrong signals,” O’Neill says. An investigative report by The New York Times in 2024 also found that some banked cord blood samples were contaminated, and that some parents were misled about their value. “We don’t know that the technology that was used X number of years prior will actually still be on par with the quality of the cells that we can generate at that time,” Woltjen says.

There are some proven, heavily researched stem cell therapies, including for certain types of cancer. But most experts don’t approve of using current therapies in a non-medical setting, pointing to the lack of scientific evidence, clinical testing, and regulations. “If you’ve paid $50,000 to go travel someplace to help your bad knee, there’s a placebo response. Unproven therapies have long been supported using testimonials and anecdotes. Good, independent clinical trials that show efficacy just don’t exist,” Caulfield says. He’d like to see more, not less, oversight. “People will say, ‘Your evil bureaucracy, the FDA, is keeping you from accessing these clearly efficacious therapies.’ But you’re not seeing as much regulation as is warranted. There have been situations where clinics have been held to task, but the FDA just doesn’t have the resources. If you layer RFK Jr. on top, the political will to take action has dissipated significantly over the last two years.”

This is not necessarily to discount stem cell–related beauty treatments or products. Exosomes, cell by-products that contain lipids and proteins and can be derived from stem cells, are now commonly seen in skin care formulations. “There are legitimate stem cell–derived factors,” O’Neill says, but “they are not the cells themselves,” using the cow and the milk as an analogy. In Seoul, a stem cell beauty treatment called stromal vascular fraction (SVF) extracts stem cells, growth factors, and other cells from fat tissue, and then reinjects them into the skin. Gabriel Chiu, DOM.D., founder and CEO of Beverly Hills Plastic Surgery, adds that there are strict guidelines for how this is performed. He has used banked and fresh stem cells from fat tissue for fat grafting, and says, “Patients have been very happy with the results.”

For people who have banked their stem cells, even if they aren’t sure how or if they will one day be used, the process offers mental reassurance. Cynthia Sakai, founder of the personal care and lifestyle brand Evolvetogether, banked her son’s stem cells and described it as safeguarding: “I remember thinking that this was something we could only do once, at the moment he was born. We could always decide later that we did not need it, but we could never go back and collect it again.” When Smith was later diagnosed with breast cancer, she felt reassured that her stem cells were there. But even she says, “If you bank your own stem cells, can they be used? Because it won’t necessarily fit into the regulatory environment.”

The experts generally agree that stem cell banking is not a must-do procedure. O’Neill doesn’t like to say “never.” But when I ask how he would advise a friend, he says, “I rarely make definitive statements like this, but in 2026, stem cell banking is not worth it. It doesn’t mean it won’t be worth it someday. But someday will not be next year or the year after.”

A version of this story appears in the November 2026 issue of ELLE.

#6725. How Lafayette 148 Became New York’s Newest Heritage Brand

What’s Lafayette 148’s secret to longevity? After 30 years in business, the company has claimed a seat as one of New York’s newest heritage labels. Co-founder and CEO Deirdre Quinn attributes that status to a combination of consistency and evolution, the balance of knowing what needs to change over time and what absolutely cannot.

The brand’s biggest turning point was during the pandemic, when abrupt shifts in customer demand collided with supply chain challenges that threatened to put the company out of business. Quinn and Emily Smith, Lafayette 148’s creative director who joined the brand in 2002 as an intern, made the decision to move the label further upmarket, recommitting to its vertically integrated business model to protect margins and avoid the trappings of order minimums that most brands have to meet. They invested in better quality materials and shifted the majority of sales from wholesale retail to its direct-to-consumer network of stores and e-commerce, with more full-price sellthrough even as prices have increased in step with quality improvements.

Lafayette 148 creative director Emily Smith.

Today, Quinn says she sees Lafayette 148’s competition being less fellow American brands and more as European luxury brands. The brand holds a two-hour slot for its presentations on the New York Fashion Week calendar (Quinn and Smith say they prefer the time to mingle with guests and clients that presentations allow), and this year, started hosting a showroom in Paris for the first time, and also started selling in Harrods last year. The brand projects sales for 2026 will be up 12% over 2025, to $150 million, growth that Quinn attributes to the luxury pivot.

Now, Lafayette 148 is eyeing a bigger US takeover. This fall, the brand opened its first store in Dallas, Texas — an investment more brands are making following the shuttering of the city’s Neiman Marcus — and has plans to open its first stores on the West Coast in 2027. Abroad, the Middle East and Japan are two regions the team is eyeing. That expansion is bolstered by the company’s first C-suite supporting Quinn, including a chief marketing officer, chief merchant and chief commercial officer.

In a joint interview, Quinn and Smith spoke about the recipe for succeeding as an independent label in New York through intentional reinvention.

Vogue: Lafayette 148 is celebrating 30 years in business this year. What are the steps you took to ensure you’re still standing today?

Deirdre Quinn: Luckily, as a privately owned company, we were able to evolve into what works for us. We want people who want our brand. I don’t need to force it. I’ve watched a lot of people come and go in my 30 years. Luxury has always been the goal for us. So we had to rebuild. Now, we live in the next six months because if that last several years have taught us anything, it’s that you can’t plan like you used to. It makes it exciting.

Emily Smith: For me, it comes down to the quality. We’ve always had really great quality, and I think that’s because we’re vertical. I’ve been working for Deirdre for many years. I grew up here and grew up within the factory, and so I just knew the potential and that we could push it even more. We’re more innovative today with our suppliers, with more of our point of view. That has been the defining difference between where we were and how we’ve evolved. And that part’s been really fun because each season you can stick to the DNA, but just move it a little bit further each season, and move our client along a little bit every season too, but not to a place where she doesn’t recognize it anymore. That’s really important.

Vogue: What advice would you give to a brand starting out today? What advice do you still find yourself seeking?

DQ: I deal with a lot of young brands that want advice and how to get into this industry and what do I think? I usually say to people, “You might not want to hear it from me because I’m a very straight shooter and I have to be honest. I’m not going to act like this is an easy industry. It’s a really tough industry and you should learn from others before you get too far down a road that you didn’t realize was so complicated.”

The advice that I would ask might be around the best way to finance a privately owned business. That’s quite interesting to me. Certainly the thoughts on being more of a global business and what experiences they’ve had in it, doing more non-sized business. We are such a sized business — we have 58 sizes — and it’s the hardest part because of the engineering that goes into making a garment look good.

The label, previously a mid-tier department store name, has transformed itself into a luxe favourite for high-end customers. How did it pull it off?

Vogue: Have you ever considered raising outside investment?

DQ: I thought about it at the worst possible times — the times where you needed help with your cash flow — and that would be a horrible time to sell the company because you wouldn’t get what you put into it. Today, I’m not looking at all. I don’t need the distraction. I have learned to never say never, but for now, I think it’s too exciting for us. I have a plan through 2030, and I’m optimistic about that.

It’s such a power and privilege to not have to answer to someone else. I know that I am a very hands-on owner, and I would be so afraid of somebody coming in here and the first thing they want to do is buy less expensive fabrics or something that just starts a race to the bottom. And it doesn’t mean that there might not someday be some amazing person or company that says, “Wow, you’ve built an American luxury brand. That’s not normal around here. Together, we could take it to another level.” But again, for now, I’m just really focused on rebuilding and continuing to grow what we have and both top and bottom line.

Vogue: You’ve described Lafayette’s customers as successful career women. How do you evolve who your customer base is? Are you thinking about how to capture younger generations?

ES: I want to take a step back to take a step forward on that one. When we were working on the 30th collection, I came across some old sketches that were by the first designer here. And there was sort of this sense of responsibility that you always have in this position to maintain the brand and maintain the clients and never change it too much. And it was really fun to go back and look at where we had started and to see the progression of how it’s evolved. The biggest takeaway was that when Lafayette started, it was addressing career women who needed boardroom suits for the office every day. And look how much our lifestyles have completely changed.

Those are things you almost don’t think about. You just subconsciously are evolving them because we are the clients. We know what those changes are. We are in touch with them. I think it’s more of a sensibility than really thinking about a demographic. We never talk about an age range. We know our customer is an accomplished woman. She’s busy at any age, at any stage in her career or whatever she has going on, and that idea of versatility and wardrobing and the product that she has in her closet is always relevant. I think the one thing I’ve heard consistently from all of our clients is usually she wants to be taken seriously. She never wants to walk in a room and feel silly or fussy or like the clothes are wearing for her. I think that can cross any age range and just making sure that we stay true to our brand DNA and all of that just will kind of translate to any demographic.

Behind the scenes of Lafayette 148’s 30th anniversary campaign shoot with costume designer-turned-model Sophie de Rakoff.

ES: Not really. Proportion and relevance are two important things for me, and technology, because I do think it affects fabric constructions and things like that. But we’re not interested, and our client’s not interested, in what’s the new hot thing right now. To me, it’s more the hemlines are up or down, little things that are more subconscious than specifically this is the statement for the season. I love when people are like, “What’s the color of the season?” I’m like, “I don’t know.” That feels like such an old-fashioned thing to ask, right? It’s sort of what works for you. You should dress for what works for your shape, your style. For us, tailoring is always more important.

As far as building and growing our base, to me, it’s more about getting our brand in more conversations and having more people wearing it, I think is the biggest growth opportunity. I think we’ve been a hidden secret, and there’s sort of a nice nuance to that. But I think just slowly getting it to other people at a healthy pace that feels manageable that we don’t ever sacrifice the integrity of what we’re doing. And potentially we do collaborations with other categories, but we’re so focused on ready to wear and that’s our expertise.

DQ: We’re open to that. I think building the brand and investing in the marketing is really a focus for now because I think that’s what helps set us apart on top of the product. It has to feel right.

Vogue: How do you plan to maintain this growth from here, what comes next?

DQ: We’ve planned it into the future. Luckily as a privately owned company, we’ve able to evolve into what works for us. We want people that want our brand. I don’t need to force it. [As we continue to expand into Europe], I think the best part will be, we’re a 30-year-old company. We’re not this new brand. We’ve got the stability and the infrastructure to support everything it takes to build a proper long-term partnership.

I am lucky that my partners don’t push me. I don’t have a board. I don’t have a boss, so I don’t focus on a metric like having to hit double-digit growth. Single digit is fine. It’s an extremely open-book type of operation that we’re running, and my team has been with me through the bad times, and I want them to be with me through the good times. We’ve had some really tough times in the last five years, and now I see a really bright future, so I'm excited. I’m more excited for them than for anything else.

#6724. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6722. Legal Shrooms Are Coming

Could psilocybin offer a breakthrough for treatment-resistant depression?

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

As part of the Future of Beauty Awards, the ELLE beauty team looked ahead at what will be next in beauty and wellness.

Shrooms are passed around at parties as a hangover-free alternative to alcohol. Zoë Kravitz, playing a fictionalized version of herself, accidentally overdosed on them in an episode of Apple TV+’s The Studio. But soon, they may be officially recognized as more than a way to let loose and could be used as a powerful weapon to combat serious depression, with the potential of being legalized in the U.S. by early 2027. Psilocybin is currently legal in some parts of Oregon and Colorado for treating mental health conditions in certain settings; at the federal level, it’s classified as a Schedule I controlled substance, considered to have no medical use and a high potential for abuse. But with biotechnology company Compass Pathways having achieved two consecutively positive Phase 3 trials for its COMP360 psilocybin therapy in treatment-resistant depression, that may change soon. Shrooms could make history as the first classic psychedelic drug (working on a particular serotonin receptor in the brain) approved by the FDA.

In an unaffiliated 2026 study in the journal Nature Medicine, scientists found that people with treatment-resistant depression who were given COMP360’s formulation of psilocybin had lower depression scores than those treated with a placebo. A Johns Hopkins Medicine study published in the Journal of Psychopharmacology in 2022 showed that the antidepressant effects of psilocybin therapy, alongside supportive psychotherapy, may last for a full year. It’s already legal for therapeutic treatment of some mental health conditions in countries like Australia, New Zealand, and Switzerland. Jay Godfrey, co-founder and CEO of Nushama, which is billed as the world’s largest psychedelic wellness center in New York City, uses a familiar psychological construct to speculate about how it might work. “There is a theory that psilocybin causes a quieting of an area of our brain called the default mode network, where your ego is housed,” he says. “Your own righteousness, search for validation, opinions, judgments—all those things are housed in ego. Psilocybin creates what we call ego dissolution: You get to observe yourself in the absence of your judgment, opinions, and all the walls that are around you that keep you safe. It allows you to see your traumas and your life story through a much more loving and compassionate [lens].”

Traditional depression medication, like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), is typically taken every day to balance serotonin levels in the brain. Psilocybin would likely be different. “You’re taking one to four doses per year,” says Myriam Barthes, the co-founder and CEO of Journey Clinical, the largest psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy platform in the United States. “The experience itself will last about five to seven hours.” Godfrey says that a standard dose of magic mushrooms could likely be 25 milligrams, and both Godfrey and Barthes stress that, unlike legalized marijuana, psilocybin may be regulated as a pharmaceutical drug, with each experience taking place in a clinic under the watchful eye of a medical professional trained in psilocybin therapy. It would be very unlikely that you could have the option to get a prescription for shrooms and take them at home, according to Lief Fenno, MD, PhD, chair of the American Psychiatric Association Council on Addiction Psychiatry. “Patient safety is paramount, so these are highly controlled situations with trained professionals,” Fenno says. “That’s very different than you simply taking a bunch of mushrooms or dropping acid.”

According to the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry, around 2.8 million people have treatment-resistant depression, medically defined by the FDA as having tried two different antidepressants and seen limited improvement (though there’s no prevailing consensus on this definition). Christopher Pittenger, MD, PhD, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine, says that there are a few compelling theories for how psilocybin could help them. “One is that it increases brain plasticity,” he says. A healthy brain is more clay than glass, able to be shaped by experience. When someone is severely depressed, their brain is often less able to make new connections and change; psilocybin might be able to make it more pliable. A second theory is that shrooms can alter brain circuits, which control how your mind processes information. One of those circuits is the default mode network that Godfrey mentioned—and Pittenger says that when this network is impacted, you may be able to view yourself differently, which can positively impact your mental health.

Because psilocybin would likely only be available in a clinic under the supervision of medically trained professionals if it gets approved, Pittenger says, there’s little risk of it being abused. “People can use and overuse it, but I don’t think that the medical approval is going to increase the ability to use it recreationally,” he says. The main worry, he adds, is that psilocybin could cause psychosis in people who are already at risk for it, like those with a medical or family history of schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Headaches, nausea, anxiety, dizziness, and elevated blood pressure have been associated with its administration in clinical trials. The drug may also slightly increase blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure should likely avoid it. A full medical and psychiatric evaluation that covers medical history and past psychedelic use should be done prior to this treatment.

One persistent problem with the trials for psilocybin therapy is that it’s uniquely hard to blind them, which means that patients usually know if they’re being given a psychedelic drug. “Patients in the trials know whether or not they’re getting a compound that creates an altered state of consciousness, or if they’re getting a neutral placebo,” Fenno says. “There are trials ongoing that are trying to understand how much of the very real therapeutic effect we see is due specifically to the psilocybin.”

A recent RAND survey found that public support for legalized psilocybin (currently 23 percent) nearly matches the support for cannabis in the mid-’90s, and Colorado and Oregon have already decriminalized it. But their experience raises caution. “We showed that with decriminalization, the number of adults using psilocybin about doubled in each state,” says Joshua C. Black, PhD, a statistical scientist who recently conducted an analysis of the two states for the American Medical Association. “The size and timing of that increase suggested that many people are using outside of the legal frameworks in both states, at least in the initial years.” The study notes that people in decriminalized states may have felt more comfortable self-reporting psilocybin use, since there are fewer legal repercussions. While this increase might sound alarming, Black says that prescription access will be much more tightly controlled than access under broad decriminalization. “FDA-approved drugs will have substantial controls over manufacturing and distribution, and I don’t think that would generate the same pattern.”

Whether or not psilocybin gets FDA approval, the fact that we’re talking about a different kind of depression treatment makes some experts optimistic. “One of the most exciting parts about all of this research is that it’s got the entire country talking about mental illness, and new treatments for it,” Fenno says. So while shroom chocolates surreptitiously handed out at a dinner party will likely remain illegal and you probably won’t be able to buy them at a dispensary, people with treatment-resistant depression may soon have a new option available under medical supervision.

Editor’s note: If you or someone you know is experiencing a mental health crisis or depression, dial 988 or (800) 662-HELP for emergency help or consult the resources available on the American Psychiatric Association’s website (psychiatry.org).

A version of this story appears in the November 2026 issue of ELLE.

#6721. Balmain Resort 2027 Menswear

“For me, the men’s and the women’s, they are kind of like one entity. I really want the men and women to be able to talk to each other.” Antonin Tron was riffing as we riffled the rails of his first pre-spring collections for Balmain, including this first-ever menswear collection for the house. “I don’t necessarily think of them as a couple,” he qualified: “but I think at Balmain the women are quite sexy and out there. And if I was to do something very different for men, it would be weird.”

Looking at his rails simultaneously, that relationship was manifest in substance as well as spirit: “We have a lot of overcrossing material,” Tron confirmed. Yet there was one fundamental difference in his approach to the two wardrobes: while his Balmain woman is an imagined character, his man is more internalized. “I’m also making things that I can’t find myself,” he said. The tailoring block, for instance, arose from his frustration with suits that were either too narrow or too oversized. Here the shoulders were strong, the waist defined and the fit flattering without constriction: very much surfer’s suiting. “Clothes have to help you, no?”

This approach was also apparent in a bodacious pair of heavy cotton canvas trousers, artfully distressed and cut with articulated knees, whose engineered construction looked more thoughtful than luxury utilitarianism tends to. Alongside them was a boxy, leather-collared canvas jacket whose pockets were edged with metal rivets: work-kink.

Reference-wise Tron’s masculine pantheon ranges from the impishness of 1990s Brad Pitt to the gothic wasted glamour of Lou Reed and Andrew Eldritch, the Sisters of Mercy frontman whose band Tron has seen 25 times. Most significant is David Nuuhiwa, the Hawaiian surfer who disrupted and drove forward that pursuit in California during the 1960s and ’70s. What appeals to Tron, he said, is less the beach aesthetic than Nuuhiwa’s impulse to experiment and push forward.

These influences washed through a wardrobe that veered between faded denim and utilitarian outerwear, leather tailoring, laced trousers, leopard-print silks, and richly embroidered evening pieces (many of whose kaleidoscopically immersive fabrics were, like the denim, shared with the womenswear). The double-breasted suiting was especially powerful, its confidently controlled proportions offering a co-ordinated counterpoint to the more flamboyant material treatments.

Tron sees this sensuality as a rejection of bourgeois convention in luxury: the class-generated current his personal temperament crashes against. His instinct is that luxury should enable freedom rather than impose rules. Entwined within spirit and material, the central filament that connects this new Balmain man and the new Balmain woman is Tron himself. “I think slowly, I’m finding that line: I’m finding the woman and the man, basically.”

#6720. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6718. Cashmere Perfumes Are the Coziest Way to Wear Fragrance

These soft, musky scents capture the plush warmth of your favorite sweater.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Few things are as cozy as cashmere—whether it’s a sweater, scarf, or throw blanket. One unexpected way to wrap yourself in the fabric’s luxury is with a cashmere perfume. These scents capture the best parts of the warm, fuzzy material through an actual cashmere note called cashmeran. The synthetic note, used in perfume since it was developed in the 1960s, adds warmth, woodiness, musk, and spice to a perfume’s layers, giving the overall composition a soft, velvety texture. Grounded in the warm woods and sweet gourmands of the season, or anchored alongside a fresh floral, these cashmere perfumes are the next best thing to a premium garment.

The richness of sandalwood and the creaminess of a milk accord layer seamlessly at the bottom and top of a cashmeran center.

Key notes: milky accord, nutmeg, Iris, rose, cashmeran, sandalwood, Madagascar vanilla bourbon

Customer review: “Santal Calling is divine; on my skin it is magic. Pure comfort in a bottle—creamy sandalwood wrapped in soft iris, warm milk, and the smoothest touch of vanilla. It feels like cashmere against the skin: elegant, intimate, and so addictive that I can't stop spraying myself throughout the day.” - Madrone

Many lavender perfumes capture the essence of the flower itself, but Matiere Premiere took a different approach, encapsulating the atmospheric notes from a lavender distillation factory in Provence. The result is a hybrid of fresh lavender blending with crisper hints of metal that are then softened by musk and cashmeran.

Customer review: “For me, lavender is a tricky scent. It depends how it is paired in a perfume composition. This one opens with a very "fresh" lavender, which will go quiet in the background, and it will reappear in the dry down. Lovely perfume, easy to wear and very good longevity (6+ hours on my skin).” - Ramona D.

One of Maison Margiela’s most popular scents blends the smokiness of burning wood with notes of gaiac wood, cashmeran, and clove oil to bottle the experience of sitting by a crackling fireplace.

Key notes: clove oil, chestnut accord, vanilla accord

Customer review: “My all-time favorite perfume. It smells like sitting by the fireplace wrapped in your comfy blanket, sipping your favorite drink. The scent is perfect for winter!” - MelB

This Mugler classic intensifies as it warms up with your body heat, bringing out the long-lasting notes of white amber, cashmeran wood, and jasmine. It’s equal parts floral and woody, with just the right warmth and sweetness from its amber base.

Key notes: jasmine sambac, cashmeran wood, white amber

Customer review: “This perfume has so many layers and is so sophisticated and wonderful. I really like the notes and how they mature over time. Great longevity as well.” - prespri_7178

Cashmere is the star here, anchoring the scent’s base and owning the dry-down, as toasted coconut, passionflower, and vanilla milk musk notes layer at its heart and on top.

Key notes: vanilla milk musk, toasted coconut, passionflower, plumeria, cashmeran wood

Customer review: “Soft, cozy, sweet, and luxurious. It’s giving cashmere sweater + clean skin! It’s an easy reach that I can’t stop wearing.” - Regina

This intensified version keeps the crisp, linen-like freshness of Byredo’s original Blanche eau de perfume. It takes a warmer turn as black pepper and neroli make way for a floral center, before settling into a base of white musk, cashmere wood, and ambroxan. It wears like a skin scent, although it’s in the floral family.

Key notes: aldehyde, black pepper, neroli, rose absolute, violet, jasmine, cashmeran, musks, ambroxan, cashmere woods

Customer review: “I absolutely love Blanche Absolu, intense aldehydes, clean laundry done to perfection with good longevity on skin and fabric! 10/10” - layla88

Carmina combines sweet and spicy top notes of pink pepper, black cherry, and saffron with a hearty floral center of rose, violet, and peony. To round out the profile, cashmere wood, amber, and musk peak through on the dry down.

Key notes: pink pepper, black cherry, saffron, rose de mai, violet, peony

Customer review: “It's giving 'date night,' to me. It's soft, feminine, and sensual all at the same time. As far as longevity, I sprayed it around 5pm, and I could still smell it on my wrist the next morning.”

Although it’s not quite a gourmand, Esplendor has a sweetness that’s not cloying. Bottom notes of amber and vanilla sit alongside cashmeran. Adding to the warmth at the center is benzoin, a creamy note with a balsamic-like aroma. Classic florals like rose and lily of the valley are stacked at the top to open the scent.

Key notes: lily, freesia, peony, rose, muguet, benzoin, vanilla, amber, cashmeran

Customer review: “Grandano Esplendor drapes the skin in quiet luxury. It is a cashmere sweater, washed in lilies and creamy vanilla, then folded into warm benzoin resin. The sweetness is gentle rather than sugary, and the amber gives it a comforting warmth. It doesn't overly project and lasts 8 hours, at least, on skin. It feels like velvet brushed in slow motion.” - AlchemyAge

Gap’s Om features cashmeran, musk, and amber woods—the trifecta that gives cashmere perfumes their warmth. As the scent develops, hints of spice shine through from coriander flower at the center and ginger to open the blend. Heavier notes of frankincense are balanced with light florals like water lotus.

Key notes: ginger, olibanum essence, water lotus, lilyflor, sandalwood, coriander flower, amber woods, cashmeran, cedar, balsamic musks

Customer review: “If you loved Heaven in the 90s, try the new 2026 "Om". It's smell reminds me of the old Heaven and I LOVE it. It smells like fresh laundry, clean baby clothes, spring flowers, all the calming things. I think I found a new signature scent!” - Samantha H.

Chloé’s Parfum Intense takes you on a journey that hits all the high points of a versatile fragrance. It opens with the sweetness of juicy raspberry and rose, which then shifts into a honeyed element at the center before settling into its intense ending with rich musks and woods.

Key notes: raspberry, rose, ambrox, cashmeran, cedar

Customer review: “Chloé Eau de Parfum is a wardrobe essential for anyone who treasures floral elegance that never feels fussy. It’s instantly recognizable yet versatile — perfect for spring and summer, but cozy enough for year-round wear.” -Beautybae01

Unlike many fragrances on this list that place cashmeran at the base of their composition, this one nestles it right at its heart. The scent experience begins with a kick thanks to a sweet and spicy mix of blood orange, Sichuan pepper, and ginger. You’re then brought right into a cozy heart of cashmeran and a brand-exclusive floral accord before rounding out the journey with a blend of woods, musk, and vetiver.

Key notes: ambrette, baies rose, blood orange, bergamot, Sichuan pepper, fresh ginger, fleuriste fusion, magnolia aroma space, Egyptian jasmine, cashmeran, guaiacwood, cedarwood, blond wood, vetiver, moss, ambroxan, musks

Customer review: “It’s a clean fragrance. Quiet luxury, skin scent that still has a silage that draws attention. Easy wear if you like musk. It’s all you really get. But it’s what I wanted.” - Edward B.

Donna Karan’s Cashmere Mist is quite possibly the perfume that introduced plush, cozy, cashmere-like notes to fragrance. The iconic eau de parfum, which launched in the mid-'90s, features rich florals and sandalwood—and manages to encapsulate all the soft attributes of cashmere without including cashmere wood in its composition.

Key notes: lily of the valley, Moroccan jasmine, sandalwood

Customer review: “It is a soft, sensual scent that has musky overtones. It stays with you all day long, whereas most scents disappear shortly after applying. This is one of the most pleasing scents that works with all occasions and all the different lotions I like to use. I believe I have found a scent that I will purchase over and over again without it getting old or boring. I have had numerous compliments when I wear this scent, which always makes a girl happy.” - Sasicat

“For me, the men’s and the women’s, they are kind of like one entity. I really want the men and women to be able to talk to each other.” Antonin Tron was riffing as we riffled the rails of his first pre-spring collections for Balmain, including his first-ever menswear collection for the house. “I don’t necessarily think of them as a couple,” he qualified: “but I think at Balmain the women are quite sexy and out there. Looking at his rails simultaneously, that relationship was manifest in substance as well as spirit: “We have a lot of overcrossing material,” Tron confirmed. This was a more relaxed continuation of the luxuriously louche and wanton glamour of his last runway collection, which itself had been informed by the Californian desert. “With pre-collection I can explore a bit more the casual side of Balmain,” he said.

That meant injecting a dose of dishevelment into Balmain’s appetite for decoration. Sensuously draped dresses in snakeskin and beautiful, borderline-hallucinogenic florals came with cropped flight jackets, while satin tailoring, sheer lurex blouses, and embellished animalier were countered by washed denim and biker leathers. There were micro cardigans over exposed bras, skirts that succumbed into flowerings of asymmetric ruffle, and lavishly embellished pieces whose surfaces seemed weathered by weeks of sun exposure. What blurred in the haze of Tron’s gaze was much distinction between dressing up and down.

This dissolved tension was more than a styling proposition. Tron has little patience for the idea that luxury dressing must conform either to bourgeois standards of propriety, or fashion’s customary cringe of faux-intellectual snobbishness. “For me, this thing with sexiness is also a class thing,” he said of the physical ideals through which notions of elegance are policed. Balmain, in his view, offers a space to articulate sexuality rather than apologize for it.

He recalled meeting a client in Los Angeles while shooting the collection in Joshua Tree. When he mentioned his last show’s desert-and-hallucinogenics theme, she cheerfully volunteered that she had a house there and used to do exactly that. She was accompanied by her muscular husband. “They both wanted to be hot, and that’s it,” Tron observed. This seemed a pretty good expression of the collection’s carefully direct hedonism. Super-long leather boots and Lucite-heeled wedges provided the strut, while the tasseled Zabriskie bag offered easygoing swing.

His instinct is that luxury should enable freedom rather than impose rules. The filament that connects this new Balmain woman and the new Balmain man, in spirit as much as substance, is Tron himself. “I think slowly, I’m finding that line: I’m finding the woman and the man, basically.”

#6715. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6713. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.
